comp: A smaller, switch-hitting infield version of Christian Yelich, same profile and swing mechanics
prime_skills: Made is a true switch-hitter with elite bat speed from both sides. Switch hitters doesn't usually have a symmetrical zone approach, and Made's isn't quite symmetrical either, he's noticeably more pull-conscious righty and stays more all-fields lefty, but the underlying zone-swing rate against pitches he can drive sits comfortably above what you'd want a zero-contact-red-flag guy to run. We have a recorded max EV of 110.9 this spring and an over 106 mph exit velocity in the Future’s Game, but without AAA data we only have a small sample size of recent exit velocity data to pull from for power upside. As of August 16, 2026, he's up to 39 extra-base hits in 103 games, a rate that's running well ahead of what an age-adjusted wRC+ model would expect from an 18-year-old in the Southern League, a notoriously pitcher-neutral circuit that doesn't inflate numbers the way, say, the Pacific Coast League does for West Coast affiliates. What's still developing is the pull-air rate, he's spraying a lot of quality contact to the middle of the field rather than consistently getting to the pull-side power alley, and that's the swing skill separating a great age-relative season from a truly special one.
ranking_explanation: Made rates as an above-average hitter across every category, with a leaner, twitchier athleticism than the profile his 6-1, 221-pound frame suggests. The separator between him and De Vries is that Made's hit tool from the right side and overall plate approach play stronger, while he also has a higher power outcome based on body projectability. Peak outcome here is a .280 hitter running 30 homers and 30 steals with a walk rate that keeps the strikeouts limited, that's not a fantasy archetype, that's a cheat code, and it's why he tops a very crowded field at the position.

comp: A switch-hitting Alfonso Soriano at shortstop
prime_skills: The swing decisions and base running ability are the actual story with De Vries, not the hit tool everyone already knows about. He's chasing meaningfully less than he did in San Diego's system, and the specific shape of the improvement matters: he's not just taking more pitches, he's getting to better angles on the pitches he does swing at, more line drives and better pull angles since the move to Oakland. That's a real in-zone quality-of-contact jump, not just a walk-rate story. The concerning number underneath the surface is that his 90th-percentile exit velocity, 103.5 mph, hasn't moved at all since last year despite him adding good weight, which tells you the strength gains haven't yet translated into bat speed at the point of contact, an unusual disconnect for a player his age still physically maturing. He's also been drastically better against right-handed pitching than left-handed for two years running now, a real split worth flagging rather than assuming it evens out with more reps. Additionally the baserunning is much improved and he’s quicker than last season, while also being much more aggressive on the basepaths.  De Vries has 35 extra base hits in 93 games thus far in 2026 netting him a max 150 XBH+ on the year.
ranking_explanation: De Vries doesn't have the ceiling of Made and has a less consistent hit tool. What he does have is foundational mechanics and a track record of performing at an absurd age-to-level disadvantage since before he could legally drive. There are some guys in the Top 10-20 with a ceiling that could be considered a notch higher with some louder tools, but De Vries is a complete and well rounded player performing at a high age-to-level disadvantage.

comp: A bigger Jimmy Rollins type
prime_skills: The number that should scare pitchers more than anything on Willits' stat line is buried in the plate discipline data, not the box score: he's simply not expanding the zone, and the in-zone swing rate on pitches he can do damage on is climbing at the same time. That's the textbook signature of a hit tool that's ahead of the level rather than getting by on aggression alone. I saw him personally handle Liam Doyle, Tanner Franklin and Yhoiker Fajardo at Spring Breakout, all advanced arms, and he didn't look like an 18-year-old facing them, hitting leadoff and getting the barrel to spin-heavy stuff he shouldn't have recognized that well yet. Since the High-A promotion he's got six homers and nine steals in fewer than 30 games, and the average dip is entirely a BABIP story, the underlying zone-contact rate hasn't budged. Power remains almost entirely projection, we don't have public exit-velo readings on him since 2024, so I won't pretend a number exists that doesn't, but 41 extra-base hits in 94 total games this year, including a six-extra-base-hit, four-homer week right after the promotion, says the pull-air angle is starting to arrive alongside the bat-to-ball skill that never left.
ranking_explanation: Willits is the kind of prospect who makes rankings articles boring in the best possible way, no viral moments, no swing-change sagas, just a switch-hitter who controls the zone like he's been doing it since the Truman administration. The touchstone here is a JJ Wetherholt-lite profile with less thump, and I mean that as a real compliment: bat-to-ball skills this advanced at 18 don't need power to be dangerous. What separates him from Clark and everyone stacked below him is simple: the hit tool and approach are already grading out ahead of players two and three years his senior, and that gap is currently bigger than the gap separating him from De Vries above him. Power is the only unfinished business, and I'd bet on a kid this disciplined figuring that out too.

comp: A lefty Jordan Walker
prime_skills: De Paula's entire profile turned on one swing-mechanics fix, and the numbers prove it wasn't cosmetic. He's swinging roughly 5% more often than he was in his conservative 2025 approach, and critically, the extra aggression came paired with a real ground-ball-to-fly-ball shift, not just more contact of the same old shape. That's the difference between a hitter simply chasing more and a hitter who fixed his swing path and is now comfortable letting it rip. The stolen-base marks with a strong success rate, are a legitimately added tool for a player this physically imposing, not empty volume, the underlying sprint numbers back up real aggressiveness rather than just green lights from a coaching staff being generous. A .962 OPS at Double-A this deep into the fix, rather than a two-week hot streak, is what convinces me the ground-ball problem that defined his first two pro seasons is actually gone rather than dormant, while he was already getting to plus exit velocities last season.
ranking_explanation: De Paula solved his own homework assignment this year. I wrote in the preseason that his conservative, contact-only approach was capping a frame built for real thump, he needed to simply swing more. He's now swinging 5% more often and the ground-ball rate that defined his first two pro seasons has genuinely reversed, not regressed toward the mean, reversed. A .966 OPS with 22 homers and 29 steals at Double-A isn't a hot streak riding shaky peripherals, it's a swing change that stuck. He rates ahead of Clark for one specific reason: Clark has not fixed anything structural yet, he’s succeeding on the tools he arrived with, while De Paula rebuilt something and the results followed - that's the more repeatable kind of breakout.  There’s a good argument De Paula could be the #3 prospect ahead of De Vries and Willits and I wouldn’t argue it based on the higher power upside, however position matters and they’re both starting at a premium SS advantage without the concerns of getting blocked by a bloated system.

comp: Corbin Carroll Light
prime_skills: Clark's whole helium story lives in one specific number: an above-average wRC+ over his last month that's meaningfully outpacing his age-adjusted expectation at Triple-A, a level where the average player is several years his senior. The hit tool itself grades a tick shy of 70 on pure contact quality, but what's actually improved recently isn't the contact rate, it's the quality of that contact, more line drives to the pull-side power alley rather than the all-fields, contact-for-contact's-sake approach that defined his profile through the slow start and this is what got him promoted. That Spring Breakout moment against Seth Hernandez's 102.4 mph heater is a fun highlight, but the real signal from that at-bat was the walk he still drew immediately after. He's also shown real aggressiveness on the bases in the minors; finally matching his sprint speed, something we have been waiting for as he has been much too passive on the bases.  Clark had 33 extra base hits in 90 minor league games this year; in line with De Vries in damage and power.
ranking_explanation: Clark was drafted for tools projection, a track-star build married to bloodlines and bat speed, but the actual carrying trait through half a season of pro ball has been the hit tool, which now grades a tick shy of 70 on pure contact. The profile increasingly resembles an early Riley Greene type with less over-the-fence power and considerably more legs underneath him. He's ranked ahead of Baez directly below for a boring but important reason: floor. Even if the bat stalls out completely, a plus-plus center field glove and plus-plus speed guarantee everyday value in the majors. Baez doesn't have that same insurance policy if the swing-and-miss issues follow him into the majors.

comp: Byron Buxton / Jo Adell mash-up
prime_skills: Baez got the call to St. Louis on August 15 and popped an MLB record three homers in three consecutive ABs to begin his career.  The underlying trend that helped him get promoted is more interesting than the raw homer-steal totals. His overall contact rate climbed to over 80% specifically from August 1 onward, a real, dated improvement rather than a season-long average papering over swings in form, and it came while he kept the exit-velo profile that produced a 107.4 90th-percentile mark, 115.4 max over that period, meaning he didn't sacrifice bat speed to make more contact. The hole that's going to get tested immediately in the majors is specific: off-speed stuff from right-handers and breaking balls broadly, a real, identified pitch-type weakness rather than generalized swing-and-miss, and big league arms will find that within two weeks of scouting him. A 29.5% strikeout rate in Triple-A against a level that doesn't have big league-caliber secondary stuff every single night is going to look different against pitchers who can locate a slider below the zone on command.  Baez rocked 59 extra base hits in 103 minor league games this year and is a major power, RBI threat now hitting fifth as he debuted with the Cardinals.
ranking_explanation: Baez just got the call to St. Louis on August 15, and the timing tells its own story: a 34-homer, 21-steal minor league season forced the issue before the hit tool was fully finished cooking. The specific hole, struggles against off-speed stuff and breaking balls from same-side arms, is exactly the kind of thing major league pitching staffs find and exploit within two weeks, ask Jordan Lawlar how that debut script goes. But an 80%-plus contact rate from August 1 onward, along with homers on three different pitch types in his debut suggests the adjustment period that always eventually comes for talented, aggressive hitters might already be underway. He sits ahead of Hernandez below purely on proximity and the fact he’s a healthy hitter as of now, already accruing major league value today, whatever the shape of it turns out to be, and that counts for something real in a format built around production, not projection.

comp: Julio Rodriguez mechanics, Yordan Alvarez potential outcomes
prime_skills: Florentino's calling card is a 36.4% air-pull rate, nearly two of every five balls he elevates go to his pull-side power alley, which is one of the more advanced angle profiles in the entire minor leagues at 19 years old, not just for his age group. That's paired with a 106.3 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity this year, an actual increase from a year ago even accounting for a spring ankle injury that cost him the first couple weeks of the season. The hit tool and the baserunning have both ticked down slightly since that injury, likely a residual effect rather than a talent regression, worth re-checking once he's fully back to full health. The specific weakness that's shown up in back-to-back years now is left-handed pitching, where both the chase rate and the miss rate get notably worse, exactly the kind of hole advanced coaching staffs will start scripting matchups around as he climbs if he can’t improve against lefties over the offseason.
ranking_explanation: Florentino's fScore was the highest of any prospect in professional baseball pre-season, and a 36.4% air-pull rate at 19 years old explains why: this is a hitter who gets to his pull-side power on nearly two of every five balls he elevates, an angle profile most sluggers spend a decade chasing.  Florentino has unreal power and angles ability for his age and if he can improve his contactability, especially against lefties then he could make some De Paula-like strides forward in 2027 and retain his top 5 prospect ranking.

comp: A Larry Walker / Freddie Freeman outfield mash-up
prime_skills: Jenkins has done what a lot of prospects fail to do after a physically taxing draft year and multiple injury interruptions: keep the plate discipline metrics fully intact through a level jump. At Triple-A St. Paul, an International League environment that doesn't inflate numbers the way Pacific Coast League parks do for other top prospects around the sport, he's running a 45-to-37 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 66 games, a real, balanced approach rather than free-swinging his way to modest production. His first career multi-homer game came on August 9, evidence the in-game power is starting to show up in a way it hadn't through the injury-shortened stretches of the last two seasons. His rookie-eligibility window for 2027 quietly reset on August 14, meaning the Twins can keep developing him at the highest level of the minors without touching the service-time clock even as they chase a playoff spot, worth watching for exactly the kind of September look that changes a player's entire outlook heading into next spring.  Jenkins has 30 extra base hits in 66 games this year and his minor league career is reminiscent of Chase DeLauter, but Jenkins has a higher ceiling.
ranking_explanation: Here's a real head-to-head worth settling: Jenkins over Quintero, and it isn't especially close for me. Jenkins carries a 60/65 hit tool grade against Quintero's 50/60, a meaningful gap in the tool that determines whether a five-category profile ever turns into a three-category one in the majors. But the deeper tell is in the swing decisions. Quintero's exit velocities, 104-105 mph at the 90th percentile as a 20-year-old, say the bat speed and raw pop are entirely there; his 32% swing rate says he's leaving quality pitches on the table at a rate that's actively suppressing his own production, a passivity problem, not a bat-to-ball problem. Jenkins' issue is health, not approach, and health is at least a solvable variable with time. A hitter who's too passive to do damage is, in some ways, a harder fix than a hitter who just needs to stay on the field. Both have real 25-homer power lurking; only one of them is currently getting out of his own way to access it when on the field.

comp: Shades of Wander Franco as an outfielder, with less power and more speed
prime_skills: Quintero's calling card isn't raw production, it's on-base persistence: a 31-game on-base streak that broke the Great Lakes franchise record outright, previously held by Miguel Vargas, and during that stretch he ran a .350/.458/.467 line with 23 walks and 22 steals. That's not empty on-base padding either, his exit velocities sit at 104-105 mph at the 90th percentile at just 20 years old, legitimately plus raw juice. The disconnect, and it's the entire scouting report in one sentence, is that the power hasn't shown up in games nearly as often as those readings suggest it should, he sat on just two homers into June before finally breaking a real power drought with back-to-back blasts in early August. A 32% swing rate is the mechanism behind that gap, he's simply not pulling the trigger on enough pitches he can drive, which caps how often that plus exit velo actually turns into a run on the board rather than a walk and a stolen base.  Quintero has managed 38 extra base hits in 94 games this year.
ranking_explanation: Quintero is an elite athlete who knows how to get on base, but would benefit from trading up some of the passivity in his approach that lead to the high OBP for a more aggressive approach that can result in more damage. The bat speed is there, it's an opportunity cost, and it shows up specifically in the home run column rather than the overall production line, which held up fine through his on-base streak. Sort that out and a .260-.280, 25-homer, 40-steal peak is sitting right there waiting for him, but we must keep in mind the crowded Dodgers outfield depth might stifle what otherwise could be a quick rise to the majors.  I wouldn’t be too worried about the reverse split issue.

comp: Parker Meadows mechanics in a Josh Lowe profile, with a better hit tool and plate approach
prime_skills: Gillen's underlying zone data is what convinced me this helium run is real rather than a hot BABIP stretch. His swing rate has stayed a patient 34.3% even as the surface numbers have exploded, and an 8.8% swinging-strike rate paired with a near-25% line-drive rate tells you he's not selling out for the power that's shown up, he's simply getting to better pitches and driving them. His average exit velocity has climbed roughly 3 mph over his last 40 games to 90 mph, with a handful of readings north of 110, real physical growth showing up in the tracked data, not just better sequencing luck. The specific weakness that's still glaring is the platoon split, he's been genuinely overmatched against left-handed pitching all year while destroying right-handers, and until that splits closer to even, opposing managers are going to keep finding lefty matchups late in games regardless of how loud the overall line looks.  Gillen has a remarkable 45 extra base hits in 95 games this year despite a near 50% groundball rate (which dings his hit tool - poor angles), but the athleticism carries him to plus results regardless - even at AA.
ranking_explanation: Gillen has quietly put together the loudest helium run of anyone in this entire batch, a jump from outside my top 40 to a top-12 placement inside three months (even though I might have been the highest on him in the industry in the pre-season). The chase rate is the number that convinced me this is sustainable rather than a hot BABIP stretch, it's stayed low through the entire climb from High-A to Double-A Wichita, and hitters who keep the zone discipline intact while their power numbers climb tend to keep both once the helium settles. He edges ahead of Bonemer directly below him on that exact contrast: Bonemer's chase rate has gotten worse as his power spiked this year, Gillen's hasn't moved even with bad angles. If he can figure out a better angles approach and improve against lefties, he has 25 homer, 30 steal upside in the majors.

comp: Bobby Witt Jr. mechanics, light, with a potential Gunnar Henderson light outcome
prime_skills: Bonemer's underlying angle data explains the power spike better than the homer total does on its own. A reported 14.3-degree average launch angle is close to textbook optimal for turning contact into extra bases, and a 19.7% barrel rate at that launch window is genuinely special, that's an Isaac Paredes-caliber knack for finding the sweet spot on pull-side contact. The tradeoff shows up specifically against spin, his whiff rate on breaking stuff has climbed in a way that tracks almost perfectly with the increase in pull-air swings, the classic tax a young hitter pays for selling out on a launch angle rather than staying short to the ball. Nineteen homers before July even wrapped and now he’s produced 57 extra-base in 108 games, is a real per-game damage increase, not just a bigger sample catching up to a rate stat.
ranking_explanation: Bonemer has done exactly what I predicted last update, converted doubles-power into genuine over-the-fence pop, 19 homers already this year after totaling 46 extra-base hits across his entire 107-game debut season. The swing mechanics draw real Bobby Witt Jr. comparisons, and an Isaac Paredes-like knack for pulling the ball in the air at a 14.3-degree average launch angle is exactly the shape you want from a hitter chasing 30-homer outcomes. The tradeoff is real too: the average has dipped and the whiff rate against spin has climbed right alongside the power, the classic tax a young hitter pays when he starts selling out for lift. I've got him rating out almost exactly like a righty Gunnar Henderson at this point, which is an extremely good problem to have even with the swing-and-miss creeping in.  I love Bonemer and his ability to get to pull power, however the increase in strike rate and significant decrease in contact rates are concerning enough that he dropped slightly in my rankings.

comp: Agustin Ramirez with more power and less speed
prime_skills: Rodriguez's exit velocity readings, a 111.1 mph max and a 105.1 90th-percentile mark last year, are plus for a player his age at any position, and they're playing up further this year as he's started getting to more barrels rather than just hitting the ball hard on a flatter path. Forty-five extra-base hits in 95 games this season is a real per-game damage rate and there are rumors he may transition to some 3B time as well. The stolen-base totals are trending down, which is not surprising to me as someone who saw him a ton last year, but that's a body-maturation tradeoff that tends to come bundled with the added strength producing the power gains, not a red flag on its own. What's improved for the second consecutive season now is the swing-decision quality specifically, fewer empty swings outside the zone, which is the kind of gradual, repeatable growth that tends to hold up rather than regress once he reaches the upper levels.  The contact rates are middle of the road, but the angles are better than plus which puts a higher potential grade into his hit and power outcomes.
ranking_explanation: Every time I've watched Rainiel Rodriguez in person, and it's been a lot of times, the plate approach and contactability have improved from the look before it. That trend line matters more to me than almost any single stat line, because it means the power (a 111.1 max exit velocity, a 105.1 90th-percentile mark) isn't the finished product, the hit tool chasing it up is. He's not the most athletic body in this system, but pure hitting ability with natural pull power at a premium defensive position, even an imperfect defensive fit, is a rare enough combination that I'll happily rank him ahead of a more toolsy but less finished bat every time.

comp: Troy Tulowitzki
prime_skills: This one's outside the Memorial Day rankings since he was a 2026 draftee, so I'm pulling straight from my own draft-day coverage. Cholowsky signed the largest bonus in draft history this summer and the profile backs it up so far, elite bat speed and zone discipline from a college track record that had him running a 91.5 mph average exit velo with a 106.5 90th-percentile mark, a 54% hard-hit rate and a 31.3% barrel rate, with 89-90% zone contact and 81.7% overall contact. He hit .341/.449/.537 specifically against velocity 92-plus in college, proof the bat speed holds against advanced arms, and he's a 60-grade defender who profiles as a plus shortstop glove long-term.
ranking_explanation: The Tulowitzki comparisons for Cholowsky started on draft day and I like that more than the Bregman with power comp many others like to use, and unlike most hype-driven comps thrown around in June, the underlying college data actually supports it rather than just the general shortstop archetype. A 91.5 mph average exit velocity paired with 89-90% zone contact is a combination almost nobody in this draft class could match, power and plate discipline sitting in the same body without one cannibalizing the other. He signed the largest bonus in draft history for a reason. I've got him a spot above where I had him last pass purely on how much louder that amateur profile is than the field around him, pro at-bats will either confirm or complicate the picture, but there's nothing in the file yet that gives me pause.

comp: Kevin McGonigle with power
prime_skills: Emerson is the rare prep bat where scouts openly struggle to find a real hole, one report literally framed the search for weaknesses as looking for reasons he's not Bobby Witt Jr. rather than finding an actual flaw. He batted an absurd .508/.634/.915 as a senior and struck out just five times in 161 plate appearances, elite zone control at a level where that kind of swing decision quality almost never shows up this consistently. Perfect Game clocked him at a 6.36 sixty, plus run for a shortstop, and the swing itself comes from a straight, balanced stance with a simple timing trigger, hard hip rotation generating real bat speed, and natural loft to the pull side without selling out for it, mid-field to pull-side contact with jump off the barrel rather than an all-fields slap approach. He spent this spring training under former big leaguer Rusty Greer, who's specifically praised his aggression on hittable pitches, no wasted takes on 3-0 fastballs down the middle, and his defensive actions have fully answered the sticking-at-short questions that dogged him earlier in high school, now grading a genuine plus arm across the infield with a strong internal clock. MLB Pipeline's own tool grades sum to 295 across the board, 60 hit, 60 field, 60 arm, 55 power, 55 run, the kind of complete profile that had him neck-and-neck with Cholowsky for the top prep bat in this entire class. The one real swing skill still to prove: he hasn't faced steady 90-plus velocity yet, and his miss rate has climbed specifically against the premium arms he has seen, exactly the test pro ball will throw at him immediately.
ranking_explanation: Emerson is the other half of this year's Rays draft haul that got real prep-bat believers talking, some public boards actually had him rated ahead of Cholowsky, a rare inversion of prep-bat-over-college-bat that tells you how clean his swing looked against elite travel-ball arms all spring. The two-way trivia, a real pitching arm in reserve if the bat ever stalls, is a fun detail but not the reason he's ranked here, the hit-power combination and advanced defensive actions at short are. Tampa Bay's player development staff has as good a recent track record as anyone in the sport at squeezing extra value out of premium athletes at premium positions, and I like his odds of becoming the next data point in that trend.

comp: Julio Rodriguez Light with passive approach
prime_skills: Sirota's carrying number right now is a 46-game on-base streak, the longest active mark in all of affiliated baseball, and it's not a product of empty walks against overmatched arms, on August 6 alone he went 3-for-3 with a homer, a double, two walks and two RBI, reaching base in all five plate appearances against real Double-A Texas League pitching. A season-ending knee injury on July 5, 2025 cost him the back half of what was a .333/.452/.616 season with a 189 wRC+ in just 59 games, exactly the kind of monster small-sample year that needs a real follow-up look to separate signal from noise, and the on-base streak since the Double-A promotion is precisely that follow-up look. He's a twitchy, quick-handed hitter whose gap power plays up thanks to genuine bat speed rather than pure strength, the kind of profile that tends to keep adding over-the-fence pop as the frame matures further.  Sirot has 46 extra base hits in 98 games this year despite the near Emmanuel Rodriguez-like passivity in his game.
ranking_explanation: Sirota might be the most underrated name in this entire top 20, and the reason is almost entirely bad luck rather than bad baseball: a season-ending knee injury last July cost him the sample size that would have made this ranking an easy sell instead of a slightly contrarian one. He's stuck behind a genuinely stacked Dodgers outfield pipeline in terms of public attention, but a healthy version of this profile is a top-25 prospect in this sport, full stop, the helium just hasn't caught up to the tools yet.  I would like to see what he could do with more aggression at the plate, he’s a master of line drives and barrels, but the swing rate needs to increase for him to develop into a productive middle of the order bat.

comp: A lighter Fernando Tatis Jr; similar build and swing
prime_skills: Walcott's tool potential is a 115.1 mph exit velocity and a stretch late last year with a .323 average with an 82% contact rate over his final month, where he actually walked more than he struck out, evidence the hit tool can catch up to the raw power in real stretches. In regards to health he’s coming off a torn UCL that's kept him DH-only since his return this year  He debuted in pro ball at 17 years old, and has been absurdly young for the level at every stop even before any of the injuries. The swing skill still missing is turning that plus raw power into pull-side loft consistently, he still beats too much of his hardest contact into the ground on a flat path rather than elevating it, a fixable swing issue rather than a strength problem, but one that can't get real repetitions solved while he's protecting a surgically repaired elbow in a DH-only role.  I expect the hit tool to develop into an average tool once he acclimates in age-to-level, while he manages strikeouts pretty well for his power potential.
ranking_explanation: Walcott is one of the hardest names to rank in this entire exercise, because he lost most of the year to injury: he has 30/30-caliber raw tools but lost some of the age-to-level advantage he had carrying him in ahead of Leo De Vries in my previous rankings. I've still got him rated ahead of Sloan and everyone else stacked below him in this batch, because even a compromised, at-bats-only version of these tools outranks a fully healthy version of most of the names underneath him. That's how loud the raw power and arm strength still are, even filtered through a lost year.

comp: Roman Anthony-esque light swing mechanics
prime_skills: Parker's swing has a distinctive toe-tap trigger with real coil loading into the back of the box, the kind of mechanism that should eventually translate raw bat speed into pull-side loft once the rest of the path catches up. Right now it hasn't: a real chunk of his hardest-hit balls are still going into the ground at negative launch angles, textbook evidence of a hitter with more present strength than present swing-path efficiency (ala lefty Yainer Diaz). The contact rates have been solid without being plus, and he's shown real swing-and-miss specifically against left-handed pitching in an admittedly tiny sample, worth tracking rather than overreacting to given how thin the overall book on him still is. The plate approach outside the strikeout totals has actually been the most polished part of the profile, real patience and zone recognition for a player this new to full-season-caliber pitching.  Parker has mashed an impressive 41 extra base hits in 92 games thus far in his introduction to professional ball.
ranking_explanation: Parker thankfully spent a decent amount of time in Low A this season, giving us a nice sample size of statcast data in the FSL.  I have also had the opportunity to get some looks on him in person.  The power has been impressive and if he can improve upon angles, we could potentially have a profile in the .270 batting average range with 30 homer power, but this also partially depends on his ability to adapt to hit left handed pitching.  Parker gets the jump to Miller despite Miller still having much better proximity and more speed - there is risk in back injuries and that’s enough to scare me on Miller at least one more time where I would take JoJo in a head-to-head selection.

comp: Royce Lewis mechanics, with killer speed and better health hopefully
prime_skills: This dude is an athlete, I had a live look on him and he’s really just a super athlete and a gamer.  A lot of people thought he would move off SS to 3B, but he looks super smooth and athletic and he should stay at SS as long as he can.  He has above average to plus tools across the board with an improved hit tool this year and a great ability to pull the ball in the air plus quality attack angles, but Miller is still pretty raw and seems to run into issues when he gets to a new level, then adapts. He’s young for the level at AAA and with improved athleticism he may be able to stick at SS if the Phillies wanted to move Trea to 2B as he ages, but Miller will likely land at 3B.  Miller knocked 43 extra base hits in 116 games in 2025 to go along with the 59 stolen bases.  Miller has missed all of 2026 with a lumbar spine issue that resulted in surgery.  Many people are ready to just throw him to the wolves, but I’m still a believer in his ability - he was a top 10 prospect for me for a reason in the pre-season, but the scary thing is Kris Bryant is the last relevant player to have this issue and he’s basically toast.
ranking_explanation: Miller's 2026 has been a genuine roller coaster, and I mean that with both the thrill and the nausea included. A serious back injury erased his entire season, the kind of issue that derailed stretches of both Christian Yelich's and Carlos Correa's careers, which is not a comparison I make lightly.  I love the player when he’s healthy, but a full year off can derail development. The good news is he was already close in AAA prior to the injury and had a chance to even break camp if he hadn’t had this issue.

comp: A Jackson Merrill / Zac Veen mash-up
prime_skills: Hartman's power breakout is backed by three independent, cross-checking data points rather than one lucky stretch: his max exit velocity has jumped from 105.3 mph last year to 112 this season, his average exit velocity has climbed roughly 6.5 mph to 91.6, and his ground-ball rate has dropped from 47% to 36% over the same stretch. Three separate numbers all pointing the same direction is a real swing-path change, not sequencing luck or a hot BABIP month. Forty-four extra-base hits in 106 games is a solid per-game rate for a 20th-round high schooler out of Canada, a demographic that almost never produces this kind of statistical breakout this early in a pro career. He wasn't on my radar at all last year at this time and though he has slowed down a lot in the second half (.217/.386/.364 with only 9 XBH and 5 HR since July 1st), Hartman is getting on base at a high clip and stealing bags when he gets the chance with 16 steals over this time period.  He has struggled to get the ball in the air in AA, but he’s still very young for the level.
ranking_explanation: Hartman has been getting to elite pull and power angles and decreased his groundball rate by 15% since last season.  He’s been incredible and I believe the power gains are real, which make him a true 20/30 threat at the major league level as long as the hit tool continues to develop.  Contact rates have more or less normalized to his career averages in the minors, while angles have improved which could make him with his speed into a solid .250-.270 hitter with power and speed.

comp: Joey Votto mechanics
prime_skills: Briceno's exit-velocity readings from 2024, a 114.3 mph max and a 107.5 mph 90th-percentile mark, are as loud as almost anyone in this system, and the tradeoff behind them is worth stating plainly: his contact rate has slid from 84% to 76.4% as the power has played up, a real, measurable cost of doing business rather than a mystery decline. A near-50% fly-ball rate backs up that this is an intentional, angle-driven power profile rather than empty raw strength, he's actually getting the ball in the air at a rate that should keep translating pop into games as he climbs. Wrist surgery cost him the first half of 2026 entirely, which is the specific reason the underlying trend lines haven't had a chance to update this year. Health, not talent, is the whole variable holding this profile back from a higher spot right now, but the exit velocities are looking good at AAA and 9 homers with 13 extra base hits in 32 games feels pretty good.
ranking_explanation: Briceno is a genuinely awkward fit at his listed position, a 6-5 catcher whose size is actively pushing the organization toward first base, but the bat doesn't care where he stands. The power arrived for good in the 2024 Arizona Fall League and has held since, even as his contact rate slid from 84% to 76.4% this year, a tradeoff worth making if the exit velocities (a 114.3 max, a 107.5 90th-percentile mark) stay this loud. Wrist surgery cost him the first half of 2026, which is the main reason he sits behind names like Briceno and Salas who've stayed on the field. The profile is capped at four fantasy categories since stolen bases are a complete non-factor, but a bat this loud at a scarce defensive spot, even a fading one, is worth real rostering priority.

comp: A lefty-only Adley Rutschman
prime_skills: Salas has a track record of running exit velocities north of 110 mph and with an 87% contact rate while in AAA at 20-years-old.  There’s some prospect fatigue here with him, since he first popped onto the scene at age 17, but that shouldn’t affect your view of his skill level.  The specific mechanical item left to fix, shared with fellow prep infielder JoJo Parker in this same tier, is swing-path angle, too much of his hardest contact still comes on a flatter trajectory than you'd want from a hitter with real bat speed with a near 47% groundball rate on the season. The plate skills are excellent and a 171 age adjusted wRC+ is ridiculous.  The power should grow as he ages and like a fine wine, Salas should only get better as he ages.
ranking_explanation: Salas was a Top 100 prospect for me back in 2024 as a 17-year-old, and the four years since have been less of a decline than a long, injury-interrupted detour back toward that same ceiling. Briceno gets the edge to Salas with a higher power ceiling and while Briceno might spend more time at 1B than at catcher ultimately and Salas could be the better real life player, based on defensive value - Briceno has the higher fantasy upside.

comp: Dansby Swanson
prime_skills: Culpepper posts a near-elite 89% zone-contact rate this year, up 5 points on his own whiff rate from a year ago, and the swing decisions driving that number matter more than the surface batting average does. His average launch angle has climbed from 10 to 13 degrees while his ground-ball rate has fallen toward 45%, a real, deliberate swing-path adjustment rather than incidental variance, and it shows up directly in the power output, 31 extra-base hits in 74 games against 39 across a full 113-game season a year ago. He debuted for Minnesota this year and has struggled early, a 38% strikeout rate against big league arms who are attacking him specifically with breaking stuff, exposing a passivity against in-zone offerings that scouts flagged as a real weakness throughout his minor league career, but it’s a small sample size and he’s good at adjusting. The reverse platoon split that showed up in the minors, better against same-handed pitching than opposite, has carried into that same early big league sample.
ranking_explanation: Culpepper ranks ahead of Rainer on pure proximity and floor, he's already accumulating major league at-bats, even rocky ones, while Rainer hasn't solved his own bat-to-ball problem against any level of pro pitching yet. He sits behind both pitchers atop this tier because an early-career 38% strikeout rate against big league arms is the exact swing-decision flaw scouts warned about finally getting exposed at the highest level, a real red flag rather than simple adjustment noise.

comp: Pudge Rodriguez light and J.T. Realmuto mash
prime_skills: Lackey became the first catcher Minnesota has taken in the first round since Joe Mauer in 2001, and the underlying data explains why. He posted a 90% zone-contact rate and a chase rate of just 19% in his senior spring at Georgia Tech, elite bat-to-ball skills paired with a genuine refusal to expand the strike zone, backed by a 108.9 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity that came against real ACC weekend-rotation arms, not showcase pitching. He walked more than he struck out for the year, a 17.7% walk rate against a 13.4% strikeout rate, the rare complete offensive season for a college catcher. Evaluators have flagged his receiving and blocking as still-developing rather than finished, which is normal for a bat this advanced at his age.
ranking_explanation: Lackey ranks below Culpepper and the two arms above him purely on total distance from the majors and even an excellent college catcher's defensive projection carries more real variance at this stage than an infielder's or outfielder's does. Catchers will generally move slower than other position players due to all of the defensive and game calling responsibilities, but I do expect him to move quicker than most.  He ranks ahead of Hartshorn and everyone below him in this tier because the offensive foundation alone, zone-contact and chase rate both already elite against high-level college pitching, is safer than any bat further down this list.

comp: Anthony Santander mechanics with a Chase DeLauter profile
prime_skills: Hartshorn is a prep bat out of the 2025 draft who was paid way over slot at $2 million in the 6th round.  He’s a big kid that is a true switch hitter with an advanced hit tool and plate approach with the knack to barreling up balls for line drives at 29.5% line-drive rate, elite for any age, paired with a max exit velocity of 111.5 and a reported average around 91.5, both plus marks for a switch-hitting teenager this new to full-season-adjacent pitching. He hits from a crouched toe-tap-into-lunge stance mechanically similar to Anthony Santander, and he's already put together 45 extra-base hits in his first 105 professional games, a real per-game damage rate rather than a showcase-only projection. He hit a 102.1 mph fly out to center field at the Futures Game this July, evidence the exit-velo profile travels against a genuinely elite field of competition, not just full-season pitching.
ranking_explanation: Hartshorn ranks ahead of Velazquez and everyone below him in this tier on pure offensive ceiling, the switch-hit line-drive rate alone is a tick above what any college bat in this batch has shown. He sits behind Lackey purely on Lackey’s rare athletic ability from the catcher position. Hartshorn has had a rougher time power-wise as a righty, against lefty, but has held his own from that side from a contact and plate approach perspective.

comp: A lefty Carson Williams with better plate skills
prime_skills: Rainer's swing decisions actually grade out excellent in isolation, an 18.2% chase rate that would play as plus for a college junior, let alone a teenage prep bat, so this isn't a discipline problem in the traditional sense. The issue shows up specifically in-zone, he whiffs on pitches he should square up, particularly breaking balls, and that in-zone miss rate drives a strikeout rate that's climbed well past what his own contact-rate baseline from a year ago would have predicted. The air-pull data flags the other half of the problem, his exit velocities grade elite, but he doesn't get the ball to his pull-side power alley nearly often enough, too much of his hardest contact still finds the ground rather than the gap or the seats. He keeps running on the bases despite getting caught five times already, more aggression than efficiency right now.
ranking_explanation: Culpepper ranks ahead of Rainer for me because Culpepper is already producing at the plate right now, a 20-homer pace with an 89% zone-contact rate, where Rainer's carrying skill is still almost entirely projection against a real, identified bat-to-ball problem. White and Snelling both rank ahead of him too, pitching prospects this loud simply carry a higher present ceiling than an unresolved hit tool does at this exact moment, even one with Rainer's raw juice attached to it.  Hartshorn even moved ahead of Rainer in my latest update as he’s a much safer profile with a better hit and plate approach against Rainer’s stronger power potential based all on raw power numbers.

comp: Lefty-only Victor Martinez
prime_skills: Velazquez runs a genuinely excellent zone-contact rate even in a small early Triple-A sample, and critically he doesn't chase much, if that discipline holds as the sample grows, a plus hit tool becomes the realistic outcome rather than the ceiling. His line-drive rate has held at nearly 30% at every level of his career, not just this year's hot stretch, and his early exit velocity readings, a 92.2 mph average and a 105 90th-percentile mark, back up a doubles-first, all-fields approach that's carried through a full-season sample. He's now permanently off catcher, which should only help keep the bat in the lineup daily as he continues climbing.  He’s an extra base machine with a penchant for hitting barrels and a real angles feel with 46 extra base hits in 105 games this year.
ranking_explanation: Velazquez ranks below Hartshorn purely on a lesser athletic and hit ceiling, Hartshorn's exit-velo readings are already this loud against complex-adjacent arms at a younger age, where Velazquez needed a full 2024 rebound year to get here. He ranks ahead of Ramirez below him because he has a longer power track record than Ramirez over a number of seasons.

comp: Jose Ramirez Light w/ Reverse Splits
prime_skills: Ramirez debuted for the Cubs on May 23 and has stayed up for roughly three months since, meaning he's likely going to cross the 130-at-bat threshold that graduates a player off a true prospect list prior to release of the list - but as of this writing he has not crossed that line. His pre-callup exit-velo readings sit right around league average since arriving in the majors, a 90.8 mph average and a 110.8 max, with a modest 10.4-degree average launch angle in just the 23rd percentile, real evidence more power sits untapped behind a flatter-than-ideal contact angle. He makes more contact from the right side but generates most of his pop from the left, a real, specific platoon-shape split rather than a generic weakness. He’s tied a career best 28 stolen bases this year, a plus-speed foundation that should keep him relevant even in a part-time major league role.
ranking_explanation: Ramirez has been getting more playing time in the bigs of late and has put forward an impressive Ben Zobrist-like super sub approach for the Cubs, playing multiple infield positions on a near daily basis and showing an excellent contact profile with speed, but the power gains he showed early in the minor league season have not fully translated to the pros.

comp: A righty Luis Arraez with a bit more power potential and better glove
prime_skills: Arias' zone-contact rate jumped from 82% in 2024 to 94% in 2025, one of the more dramatic swing-decision improvements in this entire farm system, and he struck out just 10% of the time doing it. That contact gain came with a real cost, his ground-ball rate climbed from 38% to 46% as he flattened his bat path to make it happen, and evaluators still flag below-average bat speed as the one physical tool that hasn't caught up to the rest of the profile. His swing itself carries an exaggerated, long stride driving forward into the pitch with a direct hand path and some late lift, real mechanics that let him scoop pitches at the bottom of the zone. He's added roughly five miles per hour of average exit velocity compared to 2025 and he’s hit 45 extra base hits in 94 games, a vast improvement against only 36 in 116 games last season, however the exit velocities are still below major league average and he might be more Jacob Wilson than Luis Arraez.
ranking_explanation: Arias ranks ahead of Josuar Gonzalez below him because he's already producing at AAA against advanced pitching, where Gonzalez is still doing his damage in low A. He sits behind Lackey and Hartshorn above him purely on power ceiling, both of those bats project to more over-the-fence pop than a hit-over-power profile that still runs below-average bat speed even after this year's exit-velo gains.  Ramirez is a closer one and gets the call based on a much better speed and baserunning tool, but ultimately Arias has an age advantage and Ramirez may not get the playing time to outpace Arias longterm.

comp: Wander Franco with more power and less hit
prime_skills: Gonzalez shows plus power from both sides of the plate already with a wood bat, well before most international signees get there, and he walked more than he struck out in the Dominican Summer League this year, a rare combination for a teenager this physically raw. His contact rate sits at 78.9%, excellent relative to DSL competition broadly, and his reported 90th-percentile exit velocity of 104 mph this year is outstanding for his age even accounting for the level. He racked up 19 extra-base hits in 52 games in 2025 and is already matching that per-game pace early in 2026 with 20 extra base hits in 47 games, evidence the power and contact are scaling up together rather than one tool outrunning the other.
ranking_explanation: Gonzalez ranks behind Arias above him purely on level and proximity, both project to a similar switch-hit, plus-power outcome, but Arias has already proven it against high level arms. He ranks ahead of Eyanson below him because a switch-hit shortstop with two-sided power this advanced at his age carries more long-term offensive equity than a college-polished arm with a still-developing arsenal, even one performing at Double-A right now and has a higher upside than Arias with much more power and speed potential for fantasy.

comp: A skinny Gunnar Henderson
prime_skills: Kilby already hits the ball harder than his lean frame suggests he should, posting ridiculous exit velocities in a small pro debut sample alongside top-five run times among any player who ran at the 2025 combine. He showed a better-than-expected hit tool right out of the gate too, despite genuinely poor launch angles right now, he doesn't yet get the ball in the air to match the raw juice, real room for projection remains as he adds strength and refines his attack angle. An early-season hamstring strain has limited his 2026 sample, cutting off what looked like a real follow-up to a strong debut, but the batted ball stuff looks better this year in a small sample size, though it would be nice to see more consistent barrels (just remember he is also recovering from injury still).
ranking_explanation: Kilby ranks below Eyanson largely based on proximity and injury, as a hamstring strain has kept his 2026 track record too thin to fully trust yet. He ranks ahead of Burress because the underlying exit velo and sprint-speed data already grade out as loud as anything in this tier, where Burress still has an even smaller sample size of data than Kilby to base tools and future production from - though he’s a college guy and should theoretically move quicker.

comp: Mini Vlad Jr. with larger stride
prime_skills: Burress set the Georgia Tech program record with 60 home runs across three seasons, and the swing mechanics behind that total matter more than the raw count with an open tight coil to large stride stance that lets him see the ball deep into the zone and stay short to it, the kind of setup that tends to hold up against better velocity rather than get exposed by it.  I have Burress as my number four FYPD player, having been the most consistent power-over-multiple-seasons résumé in this year's college class rather than a one-year breakout. The tools grade above-average to plus across the board without one carrying weakness outside of him being a shorter dude at 5’9” and 185 pounds.  He has shown a bit too much passivity in his first go at pro ball and I would like to see him be more aggressive overall.
ranking_explanation: Burress ranks behind Kilby as Kilby has a bit more athletic range and potentially higher overall fantasy upside. He ranks ahead of Lombard because a three-year power track record against ACC pitching is a safer bet than Lombard's still-unresolved contact-angle problem, even with Lombard already several levels into his own career at the MLB.

comp: A lighter Barry Larkin
prime_skills: Lombard's wRC+ sits north of 150 this year, real age-relative production at a level most of his peers haven't reached yet, off a genuine Cole Young-style aggressive promotion path. He doesn’t get to ideal angles for power or for extra base hits, but he has improved in his gap power and has made strides to pull the ball more which has resulted in an uptick in extra base hits with 37 in 74 minor league games this year - but this has not yet translated to the majors. He added real muscle to his 6-2 frame this offseason without the power output moving much yet, evidence the added strength hasn't yet translated into bat speed at the point of contact.  He’s young still though and he’s been the type to struggle at each new level out of the gate prior to making adjustments.  I wouldn’t expect anything different here, but I do expect a capped power / speed outcome and think he is a much better real life player and points league player than for category leagues.
ranking_explanation: Lombard ranks behind Burress above him because a resolved, three-year power profile beats an unresolved contact-angle problem even at a lower level of competition. He ranks ahead of Southisene below him purely on proximity, Lombard's already in the majors, where Southisene is still building his first full-season sample.

comp: Mini Cam Smith but playing the infield
prime_skills: Southisene's contact rate jumped from 61% to 76% this year, a real, substantial swing-decision improvement rather than a batting-average mirage (granted last year was a small sample size), and it's come while he's kept plus bat speed and real aggressiveness on the bases. His swing mechanics themselves remain a work in progress, he's moved from a big stride to a double toe-tap this year, a genuine in-season mechanical change rather than a settled foundation, worth comparing to his brother Ty's simpler, cleaner swing in the Cubs system as a useful contrast. He still hits too many balls on the ground for the profile to fully play up, and his exit velocities have climbed to 109.1 this year, evidence the raw power is real even before the angle problem gets solved.  Southisene has hit 35 extra base hits in 90 games this year, but it’s important to note he is 19-years-old in AA and has had an impressive rise through three levels in 2026.
ranking_explanation: Southisene ranks behind Lombard above him purely on total track record, Lombard's wRC+ output this year still outpaces what Southisene has shown even with the recent contact-rate gains. He ranks well ahead of his own Memorial Day spot specifically because that contact jump, not the raw tools which were never in question, is the kind of swing-decision improvement that tends to hold up as a player climbs levels.

comp: An Asdrubal Cabrera and Lindor-light mash-up
prime_skills: Level's raw power gains this year are phenomenal as he’s done it without sacrificing contact, he's actually making more contact while also hitting for more damage, not trading one for the other. The platoon shape here is specific and worth remembering, the power plays from the left side, the better bat-to-ball skill shows up from the right, a real, useful split rather than a generic weakness. Twenty-three extra-base hits in 38 games against just 29 across all of an 89-game season a year ago is a per-game rate roughly triple his own recent baseline, and it's arriving despite a still-below-average air-pull rate, suggesting real power still sits untapped once the launch angle catches up to bat speed already producing 111-plus mph readings.
ranking_explanation: Level ranks behind Susana above him purely on ceiling, an ace-caliber healthy arm outranks an unresolved power-over-hit shortstop even with Level's specific contact-rate gains this year. He ranks ahead of Caceres below him because he's already translating bat speed into games, where Caceres, a full year younger, still projects on tools more than production.

comp: A mini lefty Bryan Reynolds mashed with Ronny Mauricio's mechanics
prime_skills: Caceres' 105.9 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity from a year ago and 108 max EV in the DSL remain one of the loudest readings in this system relative to age and frame, a small, lean middle infielder producing college-level raw power a full year before most domestic prep bats are even draft-eligible. His swing stays tight and efficient, a leg kick with coil but minimal stride, the kind of compact mechanism that tends to hold up better against premium velocity than a bigger, more load-heavy swing at the same age. He doesn't pull the ball in the air nearly often enough yet, a below-average fly-ball rate that caps how much of that elite raw power shows up as extra-base production right now, just 26 extra-base hits in 65 games this year despite the underlying juice.  If he can improve angles, Caceres could be a stud and really make himself an outlier amongst the army of high hit Guardians prospects.
ranking_explanation: Caceres ranks behind Level above him purely on translation, Level's tools are already showing up in games at a higher level, where Caceres remains mostly projection given he played all of last year at 17, literally just turning 19-years-old. He ranks ahead of Duno below him on hit ceiling, but it’s a close matchup as the power angles may never end up arriving for Caceres while Duno already has plenty of power on lockdown.

comp: Shades of Salvador Perez, better plate skills, not as good defensively
prime_skills: Duno posted a 12.8% barrel rate paired with a 15-degree average launch angle last year, close to textbook shape for converting raw strength into repeatable extra-base damage rather than occasional mistake-hitting power. He carried the highest bat speed of anyone in the entire Futures Game field this July, 83 mph on a swing against Kendry Chourio, and he was the only player at that showcase with two separate swings clocked at 80 miles per hour or better. His second-half surge last year, a .326/.468/.659 slash with 11 homers, came alongside a real, improved air-pull rate, evidence the power gain was mechanical and sustainable rather than a hot-streak coincidence, the dude mashes with over 111 mph exit velocities with 37 extra-base hits in 83 games this year.
ranking_explanation: Duno ranks behind Caceres above him purely on age-relative projection, Caceres is producing loud exit velocities a full year younger. He ranks well ahead of most of the rest of this tier on pure bat speed, the single hardest swing at this year's Futures Game belongs to him, not to any of the more famous names sharing that field.  Duno looks like a future .240-.260 bat with more than 30 homer power.

comp: Frank Thomas
prime_skills: Gonzales posted a 117.3 mph max exit velocity this spring, one of the loudest single readings in this entire farm system regardless of age, a teenager producing a number that would rank in the plus tier at the major league level. He pairs it with above-average contact rates and a genuinely low strikeout total, the profile evaluators usually expect from a hitter with this kind of raw juice is real swing-and-miss risk, and he simply isn't showing it yet. He hits from a crouch-and-stride mechanism that already shows real line-drive quality, 32 extra-base hits in 91 games as a 19-year-old already in AA, a strong per-game rate at a level that skews notably older than him.  The flaw in Gonzales’ game right now is his failure to get to real power angles.  He simply hits the ball on the ground way too much for a guy with his type of raw power potential.
ranking_explanation: Gonzales ranks behind Flora above him purely on level and polish, a finished four-pitch college arsenal beats an unproven prep exit-velo outlier even one this loud.  I bumped Gonzales ahead of Luis Pena as they are the same age at the same level and I believe in Gonzales figuring out the poor angles for power in order to reach his potential more than I believe Pena can become a 25+ homer guy to pair with his speed.

comp: Javier Baez
prime_skills: Pena's hit tool has regressed this year, but it’s important to keep in mind he has had health issues all year and he’s still young for the level at AA. He put up 33 extra-base hits in just 96 games in 2025 despite a real High-A rough stretch that dented his season-long numbers, evidence the underlying skill outpaced the results during his roughest weeks. A serious dehydration scare cost him the last month, a genuinely frightening but specifically resolved medical issue rather than a chronic durability flag and his angles have fallen off to too many ground balls which is turning him into a singles hitter rather than a damage creator with only 17 extra base hits in 56 games this year.
ranking_explanation: Pena ranks behind Duno above him purely on recency, Duno's power surge is happening right now while Pena's own production is paused for health reasons. He ranks ahead of Flora below him because Pena has a real professional track record to point to, where Flora, a 2026 draftee, hasn't thrown a pro pitch yet regardless of how loud his college numbers were and I want to give Pena the benefit of the doubt in regards to the fact he’s still 19-years-old at AA and that he had health issues slowing him down.

comp: A Bryce Harper swing in a Kyle Schwarber profile
prime_skills: Fischer's exit velocity profile, a 92.8 mph average, a 106.8 90th-percentile mark and a 111.3 max per Baseball Savant, grades plus for any college corner bat, and the shape of his miss rate tells the more useful story, a 33.8% strikeout rate as a pro against just 14% in college shows a contactability gap that opened up against better velocity, not an approach problem, his chase rate has stayed low the entire time. Fifty-seven extra-base hits in 105 games this year confirms the power is translating even while the average takes a hit, and his ability to reach real pull-side power angles carries an otherwise below-tolerance contact rate into a genuinely productive overall season.
ranking_explanation: Fischer ranks behind Lagrange above him purely on ceiling, a true frontline arm outranks a power-over-hit college bat even one hitting for real damage right now due to the amount of swing and miss in his profile. He ranks ahead of Hope below him because his exit-velo readings already grade a tick above what Hope has shown at a similar developmental stage, even with Hope's extra levels of pro experience.  Even with the poor contact rates and high whiff, he’s been able to create a massive amount of damage at every level.

comp: A leaner Josh Naylor
prime_skills: Hope's second-half collapse in 2025, a .220/.345/.339 line after a hot start, is exactly the kind of split worth separating from a full-season average, and the specific driver was a declining pull-air rate, he simply stopped getting the ball to his power alley as often as he did early that year. His contact rate has recovered from where he finished that season, though his walk rate has come down alongside it, a real tradeoff rather than pure improvement. His 90th-percentile exit velocity of 109.3 with a 113.9 max from 2025 remain plus readings, and a 470-foot Arizona Fall League blast that year is the kind of outlier worth noting but not leaning on when projecting a repeatable power tool.  Hope has no splits to speak of and while the power is up this year, the hit tool is down and I’m not sure it will improve to an average 50 tool at this point of his development.
ranking_explanation: Hope ranks behind Fischer above him purely on recent trend, Fischer's exit-velo data is climbing right now while Hope is still working back from a real second-half decline. He closes out this tier because the underlying swing-path issue from last year's second half hasn't fully resolved yet in his new Detroit environment, the one swing skill left to prove before this ranking climbs back toward where the tools alone would place him.

comp: Lawrence Butler
prime_skills: Payne's power and speed both graded as loud tools on draft day, and the swing-and-miss cost of accessing that power is the real number worth tracking, a 35.8% whiff rate that ran considerably higher than anticipated entering the year, paired with a ground-ball rate that stays stubbornly elevated for a hitter this explosive. His 90th-percentile exit velocity sat at 105.1 mph last year, an impressive mark for a player who spent roughly 90% of that season as an 18-year-old, and the angle profile has bounced back this year after regressing in both contact and launch shape a year ago. He's shown no real trouble against left-handed pitching, a useful signal given how many young power-speed outfielders develop a same-side platoon hole as they climb and has an amazing 42 extra base hits in only 81 games, which is insane considering he’s still only 19-years-old and just reached AA.
ranking_explanation: Payne's fScore has actually ticked down since Memorial Day even as the raw power has grown louder, the whiff rate spike is the direct cause, and it's the swing skill separating him from a top-100 industry ranking his tools alone would otherwise support. He ranks behind Zazueta above him on pure floor, an elite-swinging-strike-rate pitcher carries less variance right now than an 18-year-old still fighting a 35.8% whiff rate of his own.

comp: Didi Gregorius mashed with Jackson Merrill
prime_skills: Pulling from my own draft coverage since Bell wasn't part of the Memorial Day rankings. He ran a 1.119 OPS through SEC play at Kentucky this spring with a .510 on-base percentage, and every tool graded 50 or better on the amateur boards, a balanced profile rather than one carrying trait doing all the work. He was actually the highest unsigned pick from two years earlier before landing at Kentucky, evidence I trusted the bat well before this spring's performance validated it against SEC pitching specifically, and I'd have him a clear top-five college bat in this year's class off that swing alone - it’s a beauty from both sides of the plate as a switch hitter and he has a ton of room on his lean build to add muscle to boost his power profile.  We should also keep in mind he injured his shoulder on Opening Day last year, missed some time and may have been playing with an injured shoulder to finish out the season.
ranking_explanation: I might be the high guy on him based on his back of the baseball card lines, but I trust the swing to play plus from both sides, which is why I have him rated ahead of several college bats further down this list with actual games played. He ranks behind Payne and Zazueta above him purely on total track record, both have real professional performance data backing up their own rankings where Bell still has none.

comp: Austin Riley with a little Aaron Judge in the swing
prime_skills: Gray's exit velocity readings have already surpassed the tracked max readings of Juan Soto, Munetaka Murakami, Julio Rodriguez, Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Ronald Acuna Jr., a wild list to appear on for a player with 28 homers through his first 107 professional games. A 12.2% barrel rate matches Junior Caminero's, and a hard-hit rate north of 45% matches Acuna and Austin Riley, both active MLB stars, not aspirational comps. What separates Gray from a pure masher profile is that this power arrived without a bloated whiff rate, just 22.8% in his Low-A look, including a tiny 11.1% specifically against four-seam fastballs, though the number climbs against sliders, worth tracking as he sees more advanced breaking stuff at Double-A. His chase rate sits at 29.9%, the one real flag in the data, and it's already trending the right direction as the season's progressed. He has a ridiculous 50 extra base hits in 107 games this year.
ranking_explanation: Gray went 73rd overall last year as a money-saving competitive-balance pick after some outlets had him as a third-to-fifth-round talent, and his current fScore blows past that draft slot entirely, exit velocities beating Soto and Harper's tracked maxes belongs nowhere near a 73rd-overall profile. He is one of the biggest risers in this rankings update as I had liked him post draft, but was a bit skeptical of the fantastic hit / power combo continuing as he got up to higher levels.  His contact rates are down about 5% at AA vs high and low A against more advanced pitching, so we should definitely watch that moving forward.

comp: Pete Crow-Armstrong
prime_skills: Pulling from my own draft coverage since Condon wasn't part of the Memorial Day rankings. He hit .504 with 9 homers, 42 RBI and 15 steals over just 36 games as a high school senior, good enough for Georgia's Gatorade Player of the Year, and the calling card is a 70-grade run tool paired with a 60-grade hit tool, the best speed-and-hit combination among prep bats in his entire draft class. That foundation, elite bat-to-ball skill plus double-plus wheels, tends to age well even before the power fully develops.  Condon is one of the toolsiest players in the entire draft class, his swing is simple and his lower body movements and snap are will generate a good amount of power.  He could be the Konnor Griffin of this class from a highest ceiling standpoint and this kid is a high intensity, high work ethic player in line with JJ Wetherholt.  He’s built for a kid and has more lean muscle and a bigger frame than Tyler Bell, a college kid already in their development.
ranking_explanation: Condon ranks behind Gray above him purely on level, Gray's producing real professional numbers right now where Condon hasn't thrown a bat yet as a pro. He ranks ahead of Crisantes below him because a 70-grade speed tool paired with a 60-grade hit tool projects a higher peak season line than a bat still working back from a shoulder injury, even one with real prior production of its own.

comp: A mini Xander Bogaerts
prime_skills: Crisantes carries a greater-than-plus grade hit tool and an advanced plate approach, and his exit velocity history traces an unusual arc, a rumored 117.3 mph max all the way back in complex ball in 2023, a 102.5 90th-percentile mark in 2024, then just a 106.5 max in a tiny, injury-shortened 2025 sample, readings that swing with a still-filling-out frame rather than a fading tool. He strung together a 57-game on-base streak during his 2024 breakout at Low-A Visalia, a .341 average and a .921 OPS that got him to Arizona's top five prospects before a posterior labral tear in his left shoulder wiped out most of 2025. He walked 21 times against just 19 strikeouts in 151 plate appearances at High-A before the injury, real growth against tougher pitching even during a batting slump. This year Crisantes was playing very well until he reached AAA and while his contact rates have been better at the level, his angles have been much worse.  He’s at 29 extra base hits this year in 67 games, but only 7 of this in 25 games at AAA.
ranking_explanation: Crisantes had a great 2025 before the shoulder injury derailed it, and his fScore reflects that gap, real 2024 helium against a great start to 2026, but a tough time at AAA. He ranks behind Condon above him purely because Condon's tools carry way more upside.  It will be interesting to see if he can get anywhere near those rumored complex exit velocities now that we have some legit readings in AAA and if he can iron out the poor AAA angles.  He’s still young for the level.

comp: A lighter Kevin McGonigle
prime_skills: Fitz-Gerald's baseball pedigree runs deeper than the box score, his father Todd is the head coach at Stoneman Douglas High School in Florida, where he coached Roman Anthony, Jesus Luzardo and Coby Mayo before ever getting to work with his own son, and that same program produced four straight state titles under his watch. Fitz-Gerald was a fifth-round senior-spring pop for Texas in 2024 who's since become the prospect nobody in that Nationals-Rangers return package expected to outshine the headline arm, arriving in the Mackenzie Gore trade as part of a five-player haul and promptly forcing his way to Double-A Harrisburg by June. Earlier in the season he began elevating with intent rather than settling for a pure line-drive, contact-only game. Defensively he moves around the infield, second, third and short, giving him a real utility floor even before accounting for a bat this advanced, and evaluators specifically flag his makeup and instincts as tools that let him play above his raw grades.  I like him better from the left side where he reminds me of a light Kevin McGonigle, but we should note he was called up in June to AA and struggled for about a month until after the All Star Break - as of 7/17/2026 DFG has an 80% contact against lefties from the right side with a .292 batting average.  The air-pull is down at AA, but he’s still hitting line drives and has 34 extra base hits in 98 games this year.
ranking_explanation: Fitz-Gerald was a name I liked back when he was buried in Texas' system, and Washington cashing in on that same trade for a second time, first with Fien, now with him, is exactly the kind of value that makes a deadline deal look lopsided in hindsight. He profiles behind the more purely toolsy names in this tier on raw ceiling, but the switch-hit approach and defensive versatility give him a floor most of the names around him can't match, a real Top 100 case by the next full pass if the power keeps climbing at this rate.

comp: A Fernando Tatis Jr. light
prime_skills: Morales' swing mechanics mirror Tatis, and the batted-ball profile follows suit, real thump paired with a swinging-strike rate high enough that an average hit tool, high-60s to low-70s contact rates, is probably the realistic ceiling rather than a limiting caveat. His reported 90th-percentile exit velocity has climbed to 105.9 mph this year, up 3 mph from last, an elite reading for a player his age paired with a 6-3 frame still adding strength, and when you combine that growth curve with the angles he's already getting to, a 29.2% line-drive rate at A-ball last year and 26% this year, there's real, substantial power upside here, a 150 XBH-plus mark against his peers, even with the lackluster hit tool still attached. He's up to 57 extra-base hits in 104 games this year, and he just posted a six-extra-base-hit week with four homers, hitting .304 over that stretch.  Incredibly impressive from a power profile if he can get enough out of the hit tool.
ranking_explanation: Morales ranks behind Chourio because a plus-command teenage arm carries a safer peak projection than a hit-tool-question power bat, and he sits ahead of Luis Hernandez below him purely on level and the higher proven power Morales is showing against full-season pitching where Hernandez has struggled a bit outside of complex ball.

comp: A right-handed Kevin McGonigle with a bit of Gary Sheffield's bat wiggle mixed in
prime_skills: Hernandez started professional baseball in Venezuela at 15 and held his own against players several years older, and the early complex-league returns back up that international reputation, .302/.375/.635 with 12 extra-base hits in just 16 games, an 80% contact rate and a tidy 8.8% swinging-strike rate for a 17-year-old. His swing starts with a toe tap and gets on top of the ball out front consistently, quick hands and real bat speed driving both the contact quality and the emerging power, and he's already put balls over the fence to dead center with a wood bat.  He has struggled since getting to low A due to poor angles as his groundball rate has increased by 20% from 47% to 67% and he only has 4 extra base hits in 20 games, while he had 30 extra base hits in 54 complex level games.
ranking_explanation: Hernandez was a Top 150 name for me before he'd even officially signed with the Giants, purely off Venezuelan showcase video, and his early complex-league returns have only confirmed that initial read rather than complicating it. His complex-league sample size was phenomenal, but the struggles at low A have reduced his hit and power potential by a half grade despite relatively small sample size.  The kid is still 17-years-old, so we have to give him a break age-to-level.

comp: Lefty Byron Buxton
prime_skills: Pulling from my own draft coverage since Booth wasn't part of the Memorial Day rankings. His calling card is easy to spot, a 70-grade run tool that makes him the fastest player in his entire draft class, sub-4.1 seconds home-to-first with a 6.33 sixty at East Coast Pro, elite timed speed data rather than a scouting impression. His swing needs real refinement before that speed shows up on the stat sheet consistently, there's a hitch in it with some poor hand positioning that advanced velocity will likely expose up in the zone.   He has good bat speed though and has hit up to 107 mph as a teenager, with at least 50 grade power upside, but likely more as he ages and adjusts his swing.  The power will all depend upon swing adjustments and what angles he can achieve once he does adjust his swing.
ranking_explanation: Even a league-average bat with 70-grade run times this loud plays as a real everyday asset on both sides of the game, that's the floor argument keeping him in this range despite real present swing questions. He ranks behind the more offensively advanced names in this tier because the hit tool is the far bigger present question mark here than it is for most of this batch.

comp: Randy Arozarena
prime_skills: Pulling from my own draft coverage since Rose wasn't part of the Memorial Day rankings. He was one of just six D-I players in 2025 with 30-plus extra-base hits and 30-plus steals, evidence of a five-category profile rather than one carrying tool, though ankle and hamstring issues cost him time in his draft year. The bat speed and strength are real, foul-pole-to-foul-pole raw power, and he's also a notable MLB Develops alumnus, a real pipeline story on top of the tools themselves.  He had a crazy .417/.491/.646 slash with 20 extra base hits and 24 steals in only 36 games in 2026.  He’s getting dinged in FYPD based on his under slot signing bonus and surprise draft position, but Rose is a really fun player and starting at an advanced high A level for the Royals.  He’s a high zone-contact hitter (91%) with some real juice in the bat with an 82nd percentile 90th EV and over 110 max exit velocities.  His swing is actually pretty comparable to Vahn Lackey from a mechanical standpoint in a low crouch with a lot of bat wiggle, but he’s obviously not a catcher.
