ranking_explanation: Health, not talent, separates Rose from a considerably higher spot on this list, a fully healthy pro debut would push his fScore projection well above where the injury-shortened amateur data currently has him. He ranks behind Booth above him purely on total speed grade, Booth's 70-grade run times are a tick more extreme even if Rose's overall tool mix carries more offensive projection.

comp: Julio Rodriguez mashed with mini righty Oneil Cruz mechanics
prime_skills: Gomez arrived as the top player in Kansas City's most recent international signing class, and he's already shown he's too advanced for the Dominican Summer League, a true five-tool athlete standing out specifically for extremely high contact rates and real patience against pitches out of the zone. What separates the profile from a generic patient-hitter is that his in-zone aggressiveness hasn't suffered for that patience, he controls the zone while still doing damage on pitches he can drive.  There’s a ton of power in the swing with a really nice snap, but he does get a little long.  He does an excellent job of getting into power angles and reminds me a bit of a smaller Edward Florentino.
ranking_explanation: A premium international bonus paired with plate discipline this advanced at the complex level is exactly the combination that tends to signal a real fast mover once a player reaches full-season ball, which is why he already outpaces several longer-tenured names in this tier. He sits behind Wood and Scarborough above him purely on total professional sample, both have accumulated more evidence at higher levels than Gomez has in complex ball - but Gomez has sky high potential - I just want to get some low A data on him.

comp: A less-athletic, right-handed Cody Bellinger
prime_skills: Condon's split by pitch type is about as extreme as any hitter in this system, an 84% contact rate and a .319/.348/.473 slash against fastballs alone, both plus marks, against a genuinely poor .111/.262/.167 line versus changeups, splitters and curveballs combined, a 40% strikeout rate on that specific bucket of pitches. He can handle a breaking ball in isolation, a 64% contact rate there, it's off-speed stuff specifically that exposes him. He's now getting real playing time at first base as well as the outfield for Colorado, and the underlying quality of contact stays real even through cold stretches, a 27% line-drive rate and a 49% pull rate that both point to legitimate doubles-and-more power.
ranking_explanation: Colorado's system jumped from a preseason rank of 27 to 16 this year in large part because Condon has started showing the power output the org expected when it took him third overall in 2024, and that's exactly the trend his own fScore reflects, real month-over-month growth rather than a flat projection. He ranks ahead of Gil below him because his exit-velo and pull-rate data already translate against full-season pitching, where Gil's own power is still mostly projection.  Pitchers won’t be able to throw offspeed only against Condon and they will have to throw some fastballs and breakers to him just to keep him honest, so even though he might be a .230-250 hitter at best in the majors, he should still run into mid 20s -30s power in Coors.

comp: Righty CJ Abrams
prime_skills: Gil's angle profile should have people more excited than the raw tools alone do, a 51.6% pull rate and a 28.8% line-drive rate this spring give him some of the best pure power angles of any young player in this system (even Eric Hartman), backed by a max exit velocity of 111.1. His swing looks the part and his hands work fast, but he reaches for pitches he shouldn't and needs to harness the aggression, a free-swinging approach that lets plus-plus speed and emerging power occasionally overshadow simply hitting the fundamentals. He's grown more efficient on the bases this year and has made a specific batted-ball improvement too, cutting his ground-ball rate by 10 points while raising the line-drive rate by that same margin, a real swing-path fix rather than incidental variance.
ranking_explanation: Gil's contact rate may always land in the below-average-to-average range given how aggressive the approach runs, but a batted-ball profile this advanced paired with a genuinely advanced plate approach for an athlete this explosive supports a peak projection that outranks several more polished bats in this tier. He ranks behind Condon above him purely on translation, Condon's power is already showing up against advanced pitching where Gil's remains projection - even with the issues against off-speed for Condon as he also has higher proximity on his side.

comp: Kyle Tucker in bigger body
prime_skills: Alvarez's swing and rotation echo Tucker's, though with a shorter path and a considerably bigger frame behind it. His actual in-game plate approach grades out better than his raw strikeout-to-walk numbers alone suggest given how aggressive he runs early in counts, and the hit tool plays fantastic for his age even before accounting for that aggression. His exit velocities back up the present power, a 110.4 max and a reported 103.8 90th-percentile mark, both plus for his experience level, though he still hits the ball on the ground too often for a hitter projecting toward real over-the-fence power.  He’s incredibly young still though at 18-years-old and has plenty of time to correct this flaw, as everything else in his game is highly advanced age-to-level.  Alvarez has better speed than his actual base running ability which is why he gets a 45/55 speed grade.  He has room to improve on the bases.
ranking_explanation: I flip-flopped on Alvarez versus Xavier Neyens when I was doing the farm rankings before ultimately landing on Alvarez ahead, Neyens will get to more over-the-fence power eventually, but the batting-average gap between the two hit tools is too wide to make up in a format that rewards more than one offensive category. He ranks behind Gil above him purely on hit-tool floor, Gil's contact skills already grade a tick more advanced even with Alvarez's superior present exit velo.

comp: A Wilyer Abreu and Michael Harris II mash as a hitter
prime_skills: Rodriguez has quietly outhit modest expectations at every stop since turning pro, a .301 average and .847 OPS in his Dominican Summer League debut, then a combined .333/.372/.536 across three levels including a trade to the Reds. He now is having a rough transition at the major league level (where his contact rate has dropped about 5% and he has run into terrible batted ball luck) after complete dominance of AAA with 27 homers through 104 games entering August, the second-most in the entire International League behind only Joshua Baez, and 47 total extra-base hits on the year, a .274/.347/.553 slash. His home run total has escalated at every level rather than plateaued, 16 as a teenager in Low-A, 12 the year after in High-A, and now a career-high pace at the highest level of the minors. His aggressive approach shows up in a rising pitch-per-plate-appearance count this year without the underlying attack pattern actually changing, meaning pitchers have started working him differently even if he hasn't adjusted in kind.
ranking_explanation: Twenty-seven homers at Triple-A with real bat-to-ball skill behind an aggressive approach outpaces his own public profile by a wide margin, and his fScore reflects that gap even if the flashier, younger names above him in this tier get more helium. He's a legitimately ready big league bat right now, and the only reason he doesn't rank considerably higher is that the profile, above average hit tool, potentially plus power, limited walks, caps his peak projection at a very good regular rather than a star.

comp: A lighter Will Clark
prime_skills: Irish's swing stays fluid and repeatable from the left side, and the real question entering pro ball was always going to be how a 22.9% college barrel rate, elite with metal, would translate once he switched to wood, and the early returns say the raw power held up fine, a 112 mph max exit velocity with the wood bat. What hasn't translated yet is the launch angle, he hits the ball on the ground a full 49% of the time, exactly the kind of angle problem that turns a plus-power bat into a doubles-only profile until it's fixed. Thirty-seven extra-base hits in 76 games is a great per-game rate given the exit-velo ceiling on display.
ranking_explanation: Irish projects as a middle-of-the-order bat, more likely the five or six hole than a true cleanup spot, something close to a lefty Nick Castellanos production if the angle problem gets fixed. His power ceiling actually tops Hector Rodriguez, ahead of him on the list, but Rodriguez already carries better angles and while the plate approach for Irish and speed potential is a tad better for Irish, Rodriguez is already in the majors and will be hitting at Great American Smallpark.

comp: Ronnie Belliard build and Jorge Polanco mash
prime_skills: Arroyo's fire-hydrant frame produces real short-swing power, and while barrel or launch-angle data on him specifically remains unpublished, the surrounding indicators, a 26.9% line-drive rate, a ground-ball rate under 40%, and consistent reports of hard contact with real doubles pop, all point toward a plus-angles hitter even without the Statcast confirmation. He's recorded a max exit velocity of 109.7, and an 82.4% contact rate this year backs up an above-average hit tool that's carried straight through from a 2024 breakout rather than regressing.
ranking_explanation: Arroyo represents the classic sum-of-the-parts profile, no single grade jumps off the page, but average-or-better across the board and consistent at every advanced level he's faced for his age, exactly the kind of fScore that undersells him relative to flashier names. He ranks ahead of Ethan Holliday in my broader rankings on that same steady-floor argument plus a bit of proximity mixed into the equation.  He rates out like some of the other guys in this tier as a solid major league regular and gets a little boost by playing a traditionally weak 2B position for fantasy.

comp: A JD Drew playing the infield
prime_skills: Holliday's incremental, specific adjustments this year tell the real story, not the power ceiling everyone already knew about, his contact rate has climbed to 71.9%, his swinging-strike rate is down 5 points, and his pull rate has climbed to 46.3%, three separate, deliberate improvements that read like a professional approach to fixing known weaknesses rather than hoping raw talent papers over them. He's bigger than his older brother Jackson by four inches and 30 pounds, closer to his father Matt Holliday's bulk, and he's already recorded a 110.8 mph max exit velocity that suggests a higher power ceiling than his dad ever carried, even if the hit tool likely won't match it. A foot stress fracture ended his first full season early, as he was looking to blow all the naysayers out of their videogame chairs with his early power production.
ranking_explanation: Holliday's incremental, specific adjustments this year tell the real story, not the power ceiling everyone already knew about, his contact rate has climbed to 71.9%, his swinging-strike rate is down 5 points, and his pull rate has climbed to 46.3%, three separate, deliberate improvements that read like a professional approach to fixing known weaknesses rather than hoping raw talent papers over them. He's bigger than his older brother Jackson by four inches and 30 pounds, closer to his father Matt Holliday's bulk, and he's already recorded a 110.8 mph max exit velocity that suggests a higher power ceiling than his dad ever carried, even if the hit tool likely won't match it. A foot stress fracture ended his first full season early, as he was looking to blow all the naysayers out of their videogame chairs with his early power production.

comp: A Daulton Varsho with a better hit tool
prime_skills: Davalan added real exit velocity this offseason on the back of a genuine mechanical change, ditching a leg kick for a toe tap, and the results back it up, a max exit velocity of 111 this year, well above what a 5-9 hit-first college bat usually shows even with plus bat speed. That's exactly the kind of helium runs him drastically up my rankings. His angle profile has improved exponentially from an already-solid small-sample debut, a ground-ball rate falling from 53% to 33% this year, and he's collected an insane 52 extra-base hits in 102 games while still drawing more walks than strikeouts, a rare combination for a hitter adding this much power this fast. Profile-wise, this is basically a better version even than what Mike Sirota did a year or so ago as he jumped up rankings as a second round Dodgers prospect (yes, I know the Reds picked Sirota).
ranking_explanation: Davalan's Top 100 placement lines up with what his fScores has shown all year, a genuine mechanical fix producing sustained gains rather than a hot month. He'll get blocked by an absurd number of Dodgers outfield prospects, five separate names from this same system show up on this Top 150 alone, and I'd bet real money a few of them get traded before this logjam resolves organically, which is the only thing keeping his ranking from climbing further right now.  I’m less of a size-ist than many in the industry (as I love Drew Burress), but there’s no arguing size can cap ultimate raw power upside.

comp: Luis Gonzalez mechanics in a light Riley Greene profile
prime_skills: Taylor was an early second-rounder out of Indiana, and I thought he should have gone earlier given a plus plate approach and real tools for a strong, athletic lefty college bat. The setup itself is a crouched stance into a leg kick to access his power, and it's not the quickest load, which produces real thump but leaves some real contactability risk on the table if the timing ever gets rushed. He's been old-friend-of-mine level productive this year, 44 extra-base hits across 117 games between High-A and Double-A, a real power jump after the promotion specifically, 27 extra-base hits and 14 homers in just 60 Double-A games with a .325/.397/.548 line and a 142 wRC+. The swing-and-miss climbed right alongside the promotion too, a 28.2% strikeout rate at the new level, exactly the kind of real trade-off you'd expect as the pitching gets tougher, and the profile would still benefit from more in-zone aggression rather than a passive, take-heavy approach at times.
ranking_explanation: Taylor was a sneaky pick for an organization I trust in player development, and the Double-A jump in power specifically is the real signal, not just more time in the box. He rates behind the more established college bats in this tier purely because the swing-and-miss rate climbed at the same time, worth seeing him hold this new level for a fuller sample before ranking him any higher.

comp: Lefty Mookie Betts light with trouble against lefties
prime_skills: Ragsdale's early knock was that he lacked thump and might profile as a fourth outfielder, and that read has aged badly, he went deep 10 times in a 13-game span this summer and is now running a .316/.441/.581 line with 21 homers and 31 steals on the year. He was part of the return the Cardinals sent to Milwaukee for Dustin May and JoJo Romero at the deadline, packaged alongside Alexander Frias, real evidence of how much helium has built up on this specific power surge. The toe-tap-to-hip-load mechanism is the same trigger that lets a Betts-style hitter stay on the backside a beat longer than a rotational swing would allow, which is exactly why the sudden power hasn't come at the cost of the plate discipline that made him a prospect in the first place, a 20% chase rate that's stayed low through the entire helium run. The real hole in the profile, and it's a significant one: he's whiffing at a 36% clip against left-handed pitching with roughly a 250-point OPS gap between his numbers against lefties and righties, a genuine, specific weakness rather than a generic small-sample platoon note, and it's exactly the kind of split that gets hunted relentlessly by advance scouts the moment a player reaches the upper levels.  Right now he looks like a very good strong-side platoon centerfielder.
ranking_explanation: The power breakout is exactly the kind of swing-decision-preserving surge that tends to be sustainable rather than a hot streak, and getting dealt as a headline piece in a trade for a big league starter tells you how the industry now views the ceiling here. He rates in the middle of this tier purely on being a bit further from the majors than some of the more MLB-ready names around him.

comp: Oneil Cruz without the speed
prime_skills: Montes just forced a Triple-A promotion, and the underlying Statcast profile at the new level is exactly why: a 93.6 mph average exit velocity, a 112.1 max, a 14.0% barrel rate and a 53.8% hard-hit rate in his first look above Double-A. He's already up to 59 extra-base hits across 114 games this year between the two levels, 37 of them at Double-A Arkansas alone where he ran a 144 wRC+, and the power output has only accelerated since the bump, 22 extra-base hits in just 35 Triple-A games with a .278/.356/.569 line. The swing-and-miss problem hasn't gone anywhere, a 31.9% strikeout rate at the new level, real evidence the hit tool still lags badly behind the exit velocity data. He does at least know how to take a walk despite the high strikeout rate, which keeps this from being a pure all-or-nothing profile, and he's still young for Triple-A, real time left to close the gap on plate approach before the swing-and-miss becomes a fixed limitation rather than a developing one.
ranking_explanation: Montes is a genuine high-risk power profile, 40-homer upside in the majors at his peak, but also a real chance he hits .220-.240 the way Eugenio Suarez did early in his own career, since he doesn't have Cruz's speed to bail out the batting average the way Cruz's legs do. The Triple-A promotion moves him up this specific tier regardless of the strikeout rate, proximity to the majors matters this deep into a season, and a lefty Suarez or a Max Muncy type in the outfield is probably the more statistically honest comp than the more explosive Baby Yordan framing some reach for.  Ragsdale gets the edge as they are both righty mashers, but Ragsdale has a better hit tool and will generate steals for fantasy.

comp: Bobby Witt Jr. light
prime_skills: Lombard is a 2026 first-rounder, taken 14th overall out of Gulliver Prep in Florida, so he wasn't part of the Memorial Day rankings, and I don't yet have a wood-bat or college-caliber Statcast sample to lean on the way I do for some of the college arms in this same draft class. What's publicly established is the pedigree itself, a first-round prep shortstop from a South Florida program with a real track record of producing pro talent and the fact I’ve already had a few looks at him in person.  The swing looks really good, it’s a simple setup with moderate stride and this kid is already built into an athletic frame.  He’s a gamer too, one game I was at he was hit by a pitch then nearly hit again by the same pitcher the next at bat, a few pitches later he went yard - oppo taco.  Lombard’s a bit raw as advertised, but he also has tools for days and has a higher ceiling than his older brother for fantasy.  The plate skills and swing decisions are much better than the high strikeout rate in his small sample size would advertise though it should be noted he’s had trouble against any pitch not a fastball.
ranking_explanation: We don’t have enough of a sample size at A ball to make large judgements at this point in time, but I’ve had a few looks at him now and I like what the eyes tell me and am willing to go with my gut on Lombard ultimately being a better player for fantasy than his older brother (who is also on this list and already the starting SS for the Yankees), however his brother has a better plate approach and is already in the majors.

comp: A Jose Altuve build producing Bryson Stott-like output
prime_skills: Williams' contact tool is still developing, but he had gotten it back close to his pre-injury 2023 levels, prior to his latest injury, a sign of real recovery rather than a compromised bat. He's got non-zero power and a quick enough swing to rack up a surprising number of extra-base hits for his size, a max exit velocity of 109 over the last couple seasons, though the 90th-percentile reading is below-average, meaning the ceiling here is probably closer to 15 homers than a true power tool, paired with legitimate 30-to-40 steal speed. He put up a phenomenal 58 extra-base hits in 130 games in 2025 and this year's pace has cooled to 23 in 81 games, purely because he's getting to worse angles than his own established baseline, not because the bat speed or approach have regressed. Milwaukee landed him from the Mets as part of the Freddy Peralta trade, and the org has already started giving him third-base reps this spring on top of his natural shortstop and second base work, real positional versatility given how open the left side of Milwaukee's infield is right now. There's a real, specific platoon signature here too, a track record of destroying left-handed pitching against only moderate success facing righties, worth building into any roster plan involving him.
ranking_explanation: Williams has real positional flexibility and a bit of a mighty-mouse quality despite the smaller stature, a good hit tool and plate approach that should play up more in points formats than standard category leagues given the modest homer total. Peak outcome here is a 13-to-17 homer, 30-steal player, a real everyday asset even without a signature carrying tool.

comp: Adley Rutschman mechanics mashed with Joe Mauer light
prime_skills: Bodine might have the best hit-and-plate-discipline combination in the entire minor leagues, and doing it as a switch-hitting catcher makes it more impressive, not less. He's running elite, 70-grade contact numbers right now in the same tier as Franklin Arias, while striking out at Steven Kwan-level minuscule rates and carrying a walk rate that's nearly double his strikeout rate. He's aggressive at the plate even from his weaker side, an 83% contact rate from the right side facing left-handed pitching, real evidence this isn't just a platoon-protected profile. The power is average-at-worst, 39 extra-base hits in 101 games with a 107.6 max exit velocity and a 103.8 90th-percentile mark this year with slightly above-average angles that lean toward doubles more than home runs right now.
ranking_explanation: The realistic outcome comps here are a more athletic Alejandro Kirk with a bit more pop, or a Justin Wilson type at catcher, though I think there's slightly more power upside given how many of his extra-base hits are already going for doubles rather than singles. The Rays have a genuinely deep catching group right now, but Bodine and Flewelling elsewhere on this list are both good enough that I expect both to carve out lineup spots by the time they debut.  Flewelling plays more as a strong-side platoon who can get reps at other positions, while Bodine should be an every day player near the top of the lineup.

comp: A mini Lars Nootbaar w/ more speed
prime_skills: Adamczewski had already passed his entire home run total from a year ago after adding real strength this offseason, a 110.6 mph max exit velocity in the Arizona Fall League and a 91.8 mph average EV, both real jumps from where he sat entering the winter. Adamczewski has a plus plate approach and his pull rate specifically has climbed a lot this year, exactly the swing-path change you'd want to see accompanying a strength gain. Adamczewski is better against right-handed pitching, though he still hits fine for average against lefties, enough that he shouldn't become a true platoon bat even if the power stays a little more one-sided. Forty-three extra-base hits in 98 games this year with a 30% line-drive rate backs up a genuinely advanced approach that should keep producing even if the power growth plateaus.
ranking_explanation: Adamczewski jumped up my rankings after adding real strength, and while he might end up more valuable in real life and points formats than standard category leagues, similar to a better version of Brooks Lee, the plate approach and line-drive angles are both good enough that I trust the floor here. He projects as a .260-.280 hitter with near 20-homer power and modest low teens speed at his peak, a genuinely high-floor profile worth weighing against flashier but less certain names in this same range.  He should be a solid above replacement level major leaguer with little volatility in his profile

comp: A leaner Carlos Correa
prime_skills: Nimmala should stick at shortstop long-term as a solid defender with an all-fields hit tool that currently projects toward more gap power than over-the-fence power, though he brings more raw juice than you'd expect for his age and frame. He maxed out at 107 mph in A ball but is rumored to have climbed to 111 or 112 this year, up from a 103.8 90th-percentile mark a year ago, a real trajectory of growth even before this year's peak readings. He had a brutal second half of 2025, partly bad luck, a .235 BABIP that flattered nobody, but even through that stretch he ran a 146 XBH-plus mark over his final 42 games with 22 of his 31 hits over that stretch going for extra bases, real evidence the underlying contact quality never actually left him. This year he's got 30 extra-base hits in 71 games with a nice doubles stroke while playing Double-A as a 20-year-old.  I had a live look at him with the Blue Jays on his rehab assignment and I was impressed with his swing mechanics in-person.  He’s been pulling the ball a lot more in his small sample size with the Angels, something to watch for in the future, but the approach has also come with more ground balls.
ranking_explanation: Nimmala's biggest present flaw is pitch selection, he has a hole against breaking pitches, sliders in particular, that's the exact swing skill separating him from a much higher spot on this list. The doubles power and improving contact skill both point the right direction, but until the breaking-ball recognition catches up, the hit tool caps the overall profile more than the raw power projection does.

comp: Austin Riley with more speed
prime_skills: Hammond was a Royals first-rounder who's a big, athletic shortstop still fairly raw, working from a newer closed stance into a big stride with a fairly level swing plane, and he's added a real amount of muscle this offseason. He was a two-way player in high school who's now hitting exclusively, worth watching how much he improves with just one job to focus on developmentally. He's already touched 111 and 113 mph max exit velocities at various points, real plus power for a player this physically raw, and as a bigger-framed athlete, a move to third base with an eventual power-hitter profile is likely with Bobby Witt Jr. blocking him at shortstop. He’s been a doubles machine this year and that doubles power will likely grow into homer power as he ages up, but we need to see a shift in angles quality for that to happen as a 50% groundball rate is not great for power.
ranking_explanation: Hammond projects as a .260-.280 hitter with 30-homer power once the doubles start translating into home runs, plus a modest 10-to-15 steal floor, a genuine power-first profile at a premium position if the frame holds up defensively.  He could be your next Caleb Bonemer type breakout at 3B if he can fix the angles and get into some pull power.

comp: A stockier Christian Yelich
prime_skills: Arguelles is a well-built lefty Venezuelan with moderate athleticism who's excellent at staying on his back leg, using his lower half to drive the ball to all fields rather than pulling everything. He has a short swing that stays back in the zone long enough to let him get to more pitches than most hitters his age, and he's reportedly hit a 115.5 mph max exit velocity in complex ball this year, elite for his experience level. The hit tool already leans plus, a genuinely natural feel to hit that should only get more dangerous as he adds bat speed and strength to the frame. He ran an over-82% contact rate in the Dominican Summer League and complex ball this year with an unreal 88% in his small sample size in low A to date with low swinging-strike rates, and the approach backs it all up, he's walked more than he's struck out at every stop so far.  The biggest hurdle he has in his development right now is improving his angles, in low A specifically he has a 57% groundball rate and may need to sacrifice some contact in order to improve his ability to create damage by getting to some power angles - the same problems and early career Christian Yelich ran into.
ranking_explanation: Arguelles is raw and far away, but the hit-and-power combination paired with an excellent eye portends a potential All-Star outcome if Colorado's new front office avoids the developmental mistakes the organization has made with prior top outfield prospects. That organizational risk is real and specific enough to mention directly, but the tools themselves are about as exciting as anything this deep in the minors.

comp: A lefty power bat in the mold of a young Franmil Reyes, huge present strength without the loft fully arrived yet
prime_skills: Frias immediately caught the industry's attention this spring by hitting rockets up to 117 mph in the Arizona Complex League, real, elite exit velocity for an 18-year-old in his stateside debut. Milwaukee bumped him to Single-A as a direct result, and he was packaged with Josiah Ragsdale in the deadline deal that sent Dustin May and JoJo Romero to the Brewers, real evidence of how much helium built up on this bat in a short window. Since landing with St. Louis he's had some strikeout problems and has been fairly lackluster in low A against his performance in complex league. The bat speed from the left side is devastating, and while he's played plenty of center field, I'd expect an eventual move to a corner, worth dreaming on 30-plus homer outcomes if he keeps adding loft and focuses on pull power to a swing that currently sends too much contact into the ground and shows some real chase-rate issues against advanced velocity.
ranking_explanation: This is one of the loudest pure exit-velocity readings for any teenager in the sport right now, and getting included as a headline piece in a deadline trade for a big league starter tells you the industry agrees. He sits in the back half of this tier purely on how far away and how raw the overall profile still is, the ceiling is a real difference-maker if the swing-path and chase-rate issues get ironed out, but there is a lot of work to do molding the clay that is Alex Frias into a legitimate power hitting threat.

comp: A lefty Wyatt Langford with less power
prime_skills: Conrad only played 21 games last year at Wake Forest because of a shoulder injury and then a lower back injury kept him out for the majority of the 2026 minor league season, but the 6-3, 220-pound lefty carries a three-year track record of top-flight production at a real baseball powerhouse, including a .385/.433/.486 line in the Cape Cod League back in 2024, proof he can hit with wood outside of his small sample size at low A this year. We don't have his actual wood-bat exit velocities, but based on a 113.9 mph metal-bat max and 92-94 mph average EVs in college, a reasonable extrapolation puts his wood-bat numbers around a 106-110 max and 87-91 mph average, both plus marks for a college outfielder. He posted an elite 92% Z-contact rate in his limited 2025 college look, advanced zone-contact skill that traveled across both metal and wood settings and his contact rates at low A did not disappoint, nor have his angles for doubles power with a 34% line drive rate with 13 extra base hits in only 35 games in 2026 to date.  Conrad has good speed, but he lacks aggressiveness on the basepaths.
ranking_explanation: Conrad has a plus hit tool that might lean better than plus and profiles as a smooth, above-average defender who could be a Carson Benge type if he can stay healthy next year.  He could simply zoom up levels on an advanced, well-rounded approach the moment he gets real professional at-bats.

comp: A lefty-only Cal Raleigh in a future platoon
prime_skills: Flewelling's power has gone from average to plus this year, and the specific driver is a platoon split severe enough to define the whole profile, he's absolutely crushing right-handed pitching while looking genuinely lost against lefties, the kind of split that points toward a future catching platoon rather than an everyday role. The silver lining is that his ability to draw walks is legitimately excellent, and a real chunk of his total strikeouts come specifically against left-handed pitching, meaning a platooned version of him likely won't strike out nearly as much as his season-long rate suggests. Split the difference between a 25-30-grade hitter against lefties and a 40-55-grade hitter against righties and you get a real, useful strongside platoon bat rather than a full-time regular. He's getting to line drives and fly balls now, though he hasn't yet mastered pulling the ball in the air specifically, and he's carrying a 109.7 mph max exit velocity with a well-above-average 105.1 mph reading for a 19-year-old with 37 extra base hits in 100 games.
ranking_explanation: The crouched, upper-cut swing generates the platoon-specific power without generating enough contact against same-handed spin, exactly the profile that tends to settle into a genuinely productive strong-side platoon role rather than an everyday job. The Rays have a deep catching group between Flewelling and Bodine higher up on this list, and I'd bet on the organization finding real playing time for both given how platoon-friendly Tampa Bay has been historically.  There’s a bit too much industry helium behind Flewelling considering the rough splits.

comp: Young Charlie Blackmon with a worse hit tool
prime_skills: Veen showed up to camp this spring having added 40 pounds of muscle over the winter, and the results at Triple-A Albuquerque have been the loudest of his career, a career-high 17 homers, blowing past his previous single-season best of 15 set all the way back in his 2021 debut year. He won PCL Player of the Month outright in June, .366/.385/.782 with 13 doubles and seven bombs in 24 games, though it's worth remembering the Pacific Coast League's altitude-inflated parks flatter power numbers more than almost any other circuit in the minors, so some regression in raw output should be expected once he's not facing thin-air conditions nightly. He’s running a more aggressive approach which got him to the majors and unlike org made Charlie Condon, Veen has no problem against any pitch type. In his small major league sample size he’s been chasing way too much and needs to let the ball come to him, but the power has been impressive.
ranking_explanation: The bat speed and raw pull power are completely real at this point, finally arriving on schedule after years of injury getting in the way, wrist surgery in 2023, a back and thumb injury in 2024 and some self-admitted substance abuse problems. Whether the free-swinging version of this approach can survive big league velocity and shape is the entire question that's kept him property of Triple-A for four years running, and it's the same question that will determine whether this ranking looks conservative or generous a year from now.

comp: Rafael Devers meets Max Muncy with speed
prime_skills: Rodriguez has a great eye and insane raw power, a 118 mph max exit velocity this year before a fresh injury interrupted his season, with a bit of speed mixed in despite a bigger build and quick hands that generate that juice. Like a lot of premium raw-power prospects, the hit tool is the lagging piece, strikeout issues that need to come down, and the batted-ball profile is currently working against him, too much of the best contact staying on a flatter path than the exit velocities deserve. He has 15 extra-base hits in 43 games this year in an injury-shortened look.  His biggest issue for years has been health, few hitters in this system can match the combination of pull power and speed on display, the problem has simply been staying on the field long enough to let it show up in a full season's counting stats.  He’s only played in 165 games over the last three calendar years.
ranking_explanation: Rodriguez has dealt with injuries for several years running now, but he's been productive on a per-plate-appearance basis whenever healthy, even with too many strikeouts mixed in and poor overall contact skills. He was a top-10 prospect for me at his peak evaluation, and a fully healthy version of this profile would still be a top-50 player in this sport just based on the tools alone, health remains the entire swing factor separating this ranking from a much higher one.

comp: A Francisco Lindor and Wander Franco mash
prime_skills: Celestin is a good-sized, switch-hitting, athletic shortstop who's shown an above-average hit tool and plate approach combination without having fully tapped into his raw power yet, and I'm especially impressed with the plate skills for a talent this raw, real feel for finding holes in the defense even before the physical tools fully mature. He's a true switch hitter with a longer but still solid enough swing against right-handers to access gap power, while from the right side against lefties he makes better contact and manages both more barrels and higher exit velocities. He's increasing his line-drive and pull rates this year with a much-improved plate approach, and he posted a 104 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity in 2025, essentially major league average, with unofficial readings north of 110 in the past, real power still waiting to show up more consistently in games. Celestin has struggled in AA after what looked like his breakout season in high A, but he’s still relatively young for AA at 20-years-old and has had bad batted ball luck to go along with his reduced contact rates (76% at high A and 67% at AA).
ranking_explanation: Celestin has battled injuries over the last couple of years, including a power-sapping broken hamate bone, exactly the kind of specific medical detail that explains a power tool lagging behind an already-advanced hit tool and approach. He's still only 20 despite feeling like a longer-tenured name on prospect lists.  There’s likely to be some prospect fatigue with him as he seemingly takes longer than most prospects to adjust to each new level after promotion, but overall he’s still putting up an impressive season.

comp: Michael Harris II w/ an Ohtani stance
prime_skills: Pulling from my own draft coverage since Curiel wasn't part of the Memorial Day rankings. He hit .353/.431/.526 with six homers this spring as a draft-eligible sophomore, and the calling card is the best pure contact skills in his entire draft class, he simply doesn't miss the barrel. He has plus speed, covers center field well with an average arm, and the 6-2, 190 frame still has room to add power as he matures physically without sacrificing any of that contact ability, and LSU's national title run this year gave him a platform, the swing held up against the best pitching in the country in the biggest games of the college season. He also performed well in Cape Cod League competition the summer before his draft year, evidence the hit tool holds up against advanced arms with a wood bat, not just aluminum-aided college numbers, and his in-zone contact rate specifically graded out as one of the best marks among any qualified hitter in that league.
ranking_explanation: A premium hit-tool college outfielder with speed and defensive value, exactly the profile that tends to move fast once a real pro sample exists to confirm it. He sits in the middle of this tier purely on zero professional innings played, the underlying college performance against elite competition compares favorably to more experienced names in this same range.

comp: Francisco Lindor Super Light
prime_skills: Rojas is a switch-armed, right-handed-hitting shortstop out of the Dominican Republic who's shown real thump this year, a tracked 108.5 mph exit velocity and a 30-degree launch angle on a 437-foot homer this spring, legitimate top-of-the-scale power for a lean 5-11, 150-pound frame that still has real room to fill out. Rojas was traded to the Mets in the Clay Holmes deal and is a jack of all trades middle infielder consistently playing above age-to-level and has room in the frame to add strength behind an already-loud exit-velocity ceiling. He has been in and around my Top 150 rankings for the last two years and profiles above average across the board similar to Michael Arroyo with the Mariners and only runs a slightly above average angles profile.
ranking_explanation: A lean-framed shortstop already producing top-of-the-scale exit velocities on contact is exactly the kind of profile that tends to keep climbing as strength gets added, the power output relative to a 150-pound frame is the real headline here. Rojas just turned 21-years-old and will obviously be moving off shortstop long term with the real Francisco Lindor locked in at SS on the big league club.

comp: Curtis Granderson
prime_skills: Davidson is a toolsy, undrafted outfielder with a solid plate approach from a lefty toe-tap-to-lunge stance, developing a real hit tool as he's climbed levels. He's slightly below average in pure contactability, but he carries excellent line-drive angles, above-average speed and a potential plus power tool, a 112 mph max exit velocity, a very good 106 mph 90th-percentile mark last year, and an elite 78.9 mph bat speed reading. His personal XBH-plus number sits well above average, 41 extra-base hits in 114 games last year against 47 in 105 games this year as he is completely destroying in the PCL with 16 extra base hits in his 32 AAA games. Going undrafted entirely before signing as a free agent makes this an especially notable helium story, plus tools this loud almost never slip through an entire draft without a single team calling his name.  Davidson is underrated and could be in the bigs by the time this article is released, however he is still hitting the ball on the ground 10-15% more than we would like and has to focus on adjusting his angles to create damage.
ranking_explanation: Davidson is one of the more under-the-radar breakout names from last year, and this season has been the real show-me test of whether that breakout holds up rather than fades as a one-year outlier. If he’s going to be a big league regular, he needs to work out the poor angle in order to get to his power and it's worth remembering San Francisco's home park is genuinely rough on left-handed power, a real park-factor drag on his eventual major league production regardless of how the underlying tools develop.

comp: Switch-hitting William Contreras
prime_skills: Bernal is a switch-hitting catcher out of Panama who's knocking on the major league door right now and would likely be up on any other major league team outside of Missouri, but the Cardinals are loaded at catcher. He's a Minor League Gold Glove winner behind the plate, real defensive polish to go with the switch-hit bat, and the specific thing that separates him from other close-to-the-majors catching prospects is a strikeout rate that runs meaningfully lower than a big league comparable like Jimmy Crooks managed in his own recent Triple-A-to-majors transition, a real signal the bat-to-ball skill should translate more smoothly than most call-ups his profile. He signed as an international free agent back in January 2021 and has climbed every rung of the Cardinals system methodically since, a five-year developmental arc that's about as textbook as a catching prospect's path gets.  Bernal has no red flags in his profile at all and looks to be a solid all-around hitter with top of the line defensive prowess with 37 extra base hits in 95 games including an above average angles profile.
ranking_explanation: The Cardinals already have Ivan Herrera, Jimmy Crooks and Pedro Pages on the active roster, a crowded catching picture that's the real reason Bernal hasn't gotten the call yet rather than anything about his own readiness. Bernal is the most likely of all these players to stick as the primary catcher as the best defensive player of the bunch behind the plate.  Look for the Cardinals to make an off-season move to clear room for Bernal at the position longer term.

comp: Trea Turner Light
prime_skills: Hall is a speed-first prep athlete who dominated at Complex league, but has struggled at low A with near unplayable exit velocities and poor contact rates.  Hall has blazing speed, which makes him worth rostering as long as he can start hitting the ball with authority at full-season ball. He's lean, but he should get to more power as he matures, as he tends to get out in front of the ball with a quick break out of the box that speaks to advanced bat speed for his age. He's nailed a 110.9 mph max exit velocity down in complex ball this year, solid evidence there's more juice in the bat than expected for a pure speed-tools prospect against his horrid low A EVs and barrel ability thus far. Contact is sub par, even in complex ball, though the angles are leaning plus, he's pulling the ball in the air with a near-25% line-drive rate. Hall has shown the ability to take a walk even though the swinging-strike rate is a specific flag worth tracking as he climbs and I hope to get eyes on him before the end of the minor league season.  Hall has 35 extra base hits in 77 games, but only 5 have come at full-season ball in 19 games.
ranking_explanation: Hall is intriguing thanks to the speed profile, the pedigree, and some scouting friends whose opinion on him I trust a great deal. We only have a small sample size of data and I haven't seen him in person yet, both honest limitations on how confidently I can rank him right now, but I'm looking forward to an in-person look and once we get another month of sample size data where the picture should sharpen fast.

comp: Riley Greene
prime_skills: Pulling from my own draft coverage since Grindlinger wasn't part of the Memorial Day rankings. He profiles as a true two-way prep talent, though the Angels have already committed to him as an outfielder given a fringe arm that wouldn't have held up at short long-term. The lefty stroke is smooth and repeatable out of an open stance with a precise toe-tap trigger, and the hands are loose enough to generate outstanding bat speed, 75.2 mph by biomechanical sensor, with 24.0 mph hand speed and a peak exit velocity of 101.5, that translated to a 1.000 OPS and a .376 average in his championship senior season. He's still just 17 after reclassifying up a class, so there's plenty of physical projection left in that frame on top of an already-advanced swing, an uncommon pairing of present bat speed and remaining physical ceiling.
ranking_explanation: An advanced-bat-speed prep outfielder with plenty of physical projection left given how young he is relative to his class is exactly the profile that tends to move once actual professional at-bats start accumulating. He sits in the back half of this tier purely on zero pro innings, the underlying biomechanical data compares favorably to more experienced names in this same range. I have the least amount of data on him than anyone in these rankings, but I have watched a decent amount of video as he was one of my favorite prep guys entering the 2026 draft.

comp: Charlie Blackmon w/ worse hit / too much hand movement
prime_skills: Farmelo is a big, long-levered lefty with power-speed potential and quick bat speed, he coils up as the pitch arrives and unleashes into driving contact that should produce a big doubles profile even before the over-the-fence power fully shows up. He hasn't been the same player since a 2024 injury interrupted his development, but the contact is meaningfully better this year than last, and he's getting into better pull angles as a result, 46 extra-base hits in 111 games is above-average production, good for a 127 XBH-plus mark relative to his peers. The plate approach has also improved from a year ago, though he's still striking out too much and hasn't yet translated the doubles power into home run power, his max recorded exit velocity of 109.2 from last year's Arizona Fall League is above-average but not the loudest raw juice in this system. He's fast, but he hasn't run the bases well this year specifically, poor reads and jumps rather than a speed problem, and that's limiting the ceiling of an otherwise well-rounded tool set.
ranking_explanation: Farmelo has a ton of tools and hasn't yet put them all together in the same season, the power from 2025, the contact and angles from 2024, and the plate approach and speed from this year all showing up simultaneously would make him a monster. Until that convergence happens, he rates as a talented but incomplete prospect, the ceiling justifies patience even as the floor stays murky.

comp: Tyler Soderstrom as a hitter
prime_skills: Neyens is a huge kid out of high school at 6-4, 210, who's already registered exit velocities over 110 mph as a teenager, an outstanding reading for his experience level, including a 116 mph peak that confirms the power projection is well-founded. He was committed to Oregon State before signing, and the profile is major power potential paired with a below-average-to-solid hit tool right now, the contact rates are sub-par and he isn't getting the ball in the air as much as a true power hitter should, nor are the pull rates fully there yet, though he is finding line drives. He oddly has just twenty nine extra-base hits in 93 games despite the exit-velo ceiling, and he keeps running on the bases despite a low success rate, more aggression than efficiency at this stage.  He has a pretty low swinging strike rate for his strikeout total and he’s been way too passive with an incredibly low 29% swing rate this year - so I don’t really know what to make of his plate approach.
ranking_explanation: Neyens shares some similarities with Ethan Holliday elsewhere on this list, minus the celebrity of being Jackson's brother and Matt's son, and his power upside might even be a tick higher than Holliday's given a swinging-strike rate of just 9%, an uncommonly low number for a hitter this physically imposing, which suggests the strikeouts should come down as he matures. He should settle at third base long-term, a position that's a fantasy wasteland across the sport right now, which should help push him up rankings ahead of comparable bats at more crowded positions.

comp: A lefty Rhys Hoskins
prime_skills: Burke has completely erased any hit-versus-power questions this year and turned into one half of the best power tandem in the entire minors alongside fellow former Vol Andrew Fischer up in the top 100. He's up to 31 homers and a .929 OPS built on legitimate 108.8 mph 90th-percentile exit velocity readings from a year ago that have only grown louder since. None of this should surprise anyone who tracked the underlying data last year, he posted that same elite exit velo profile at High-A but only hit five homers in 408 plate appearances because his ground-ball rate sat at 52.4%, all that raw juice buried into the dirt. Once he got to Double-A and started lifting the ball, that rate dropped to 42.4% and the power arrived on schedule, and it's carried straight through this season without any sign of regression.  He's still a well below-average runner profile on paper, though I'll flag that the box score has him with 25 steals this year. Defensively he's better than his 6-3, 236 frame suggests, soft hands and solid reactions at first, an average or better glove there. This is about as pure a bat-carries-everything profile as this system has, but the bat is now doing exactly what the underlying data always promised it could.
ranking_explanation: This is about as pure a bat-carries-everything profile as this system has, well below-average speed and a 30-grade run tool that's more opportunism than actual wheels, but the bat is now doing exactly what the underlying exit-velo data always promised it could. He rates ahead of several more toolsy names in this tier purely because the power is already fully translated into games, not still projected - though a first base only profile limits him to one defensive position or DH, so he really needs to hit.

comp: SS Nico Hoerner w/ more power potential
prime_skills: Houston was the 16th overall pick last year out of Wake Forest, and the carrying trait from day one has been the glove, a true shortstop who's athletic enough that evaluators think he could handle the position in the majors right now if he had to. Early in his first full pro season the underlying data actually told a worrying story, he was hitting .370 at one point but running a poor .259 xwOBA with a 90th-percentile exit velocity of just 96.2 mph and pulling the ball in the air at only a 12th-percentile rate, meaning the average was mostly empty, BABIP-driven contact. Since then he's turned that into legitimate production rather than a mirage, he's now hitting .320/.400/.461 at Double-A Wichita, sixth-best average among all shortstops in the minors, after climbing from High-A on the strength of a five-hit game in June. The speed is legitimate and efficient, 49 steals against just eight times caught, and the swing itself, short, direct, hands staying inside the ball on a level path, is a near-exact mechanical match for Nico Hoerner's, contact-over-power by design rather than a limitation. Houston has 39 extra base hits in 101 games and the extra base hit production has only improved as he’s gone up levels.
ranking_explanation: Minnesota has a distinct organizational need at the position too, bottom-five in the league in defensive value at shortstop since last year, so the runway to playing time is wide open if Houston keeps hitting like this. The empty-average red flag from earlier this year is the one thing worth remembering before getting too aggressive with this ranking, the underlying exit velo needs to keep climbing at Double-A the way the early results suggest it has.

comp: Daniel Murphy
prime_skills: Sitting at an elite 93.4 mph average exit velocity, 97th percentile in college ball, with a 56.8% hard-hit rate and a 114-plus mph max EV, Hacopian flashes 55-grade raw power. The bat-to-ball skills are the true separator though, an 85.6% overall contact rate that actually improved against SEC arms in 2026, a 95% fastball contact rate, a microscopic 9% whiff rate, and an 8-to-9.1% chase rate showing he rarely expands the zone chasing pitcher's pitches, an uncommon combination of elite exit velo and elite plate discipline in the same college bat.
ranking_explanation: A 6-1, 210-pound college bat with plate discipline and exit velocity both grading elite is about as safe a college performer as this entire draft class offered, there's no swing flaw to point to, just an advanced hitter who controls the strike zone as well as anyone in his class. He sits in the middle of this tier purely on zero professional innings, the underlying college data compares favorably to more experienced names in this range.

comp: Eugenio Suarez
prime_skills: Aloy is a comp-round first-rounder who fell to Baltimore and is best known for his breakout 2025 season, where the power fully came to life. He's got solid plate skills but a sub-par hit tool that will need work maximizing angles to optimize the power in pro ball; the angles he's shown in his small pro sample were solid despite spraying to the opposite field more than I'd recommend for a hitter with this much strength. There's no publicly available wood-bat exit-velocity data for him yet, but he maxed at 114 mph with metal and had a standout Cape Cod League performance in 2024, eight home runs, before his Arkansas breakout the following spring, telling evidence there weren't any transition issues moving between bat types. He's got a simple toe-tap setup in the box, and that mechanical simplicity should lead to a consistent overall approach as he climbs, oddly he has just as many home runs as doubles this year with 42 extra-base hits in 107 games.
ranking_explanation: Aloy was dominant through his small Low-A sample, which tracks given he was the 2025 Golden Spikes winner, telling evidence against the best amateur competition in the country. He should be a quick mover if he can reign in the opposite-field spraying and start pulling more of his hardest contact in the air, that specific angle adjustment plus getting the ball off the ground is the swing skill separating him from a much higher ranking.

comp: Righty only Carlos Santana
prime_skills: Ramirez has a beautiful swing and does an outstanding job keeping his hands back, leading to a potential plus hit-and-power combination from the catcher position. He hit a 109 mph home run in this year's Spring Breakout game, and he's since reached a max exit velocity of 113.4 as a pro while logging an approximate 105 mph 90th-percentile EV, both plus marks for a 20-year-old catcher. His contact rate is up this year from last, including tangible gains getting to better angles, a 26.8% line-drive rate and increased pull power, and he has 35 extra-base hits in 75 games, though he's sacrificed a bit of his plate approach in the process, walking a little less than his own established baseline.  He’s been hurt since July 17th with an undisclosed injury, but he was having a great year up until that point.
ranking_explanation: Ramirez does an outstanding job getting into power with a controlled swing that generates an above-average number of extra-base hits, a 137 XBH-plus mark relative to his peers. The exit velocities confirm the power is well earned, and he grades out as a hit-first, middle-of-the-order bat who can also catch, a plausible .245 to .265 hitter with mid-20s home run totals at peak. Ramirez is one of the more underrated prospects in the minors.

comp: Raw Konnor Griffin Lite
prime_skills: Renteria signed as the Phillies' top international target this cycle out of Venezuela at 17 years old and son of former big leaguer, Edgar Renteria. He's a right-handed hitter built around advanced bat speed and a mature understanding of the strike zone for his age, a toolsy hitter who pairs zone control with plus-plus raw power projection (up to 113 max EV as a 17-year-old kid), an unusual combination for an amateur bat this young. He put that power on display in a Venezuelan home run derby recently, 18 bombs in the event, notably outslugging Royals catcher Salvador Perez's own showing in the same competition.  Renteria absolutely destroyed the DSL this year and has since moved to the bridge league and has been impressing anyone who sees him in the level where we get random video and no data.  Renteria had 29 extra base hits in 53 games including 11 bombs, 9 triples and 24 steals.
ranking_explanation: Holding him at a placeholder spot reflecting the international pedigree and bat-speed reports rather than inventing tool grades I can't back with actual professional data yet, he hasn't played an official pro game as of this writing.

comp: Garry Sheffield as a catcher
prime_skills: Primera is a bit of a freak with a quiet toe tap on the lower half, but he brings back the Gary Sheffield bat waggle on the upper half with some ridiculously advanced contact skills for his age that have translated from Complex to low A without a hitch.  He has a nice feel for pull angles, but his groundball rate has inflated from a beautiful 35% in complex to 55% in low A.  Primera cost the Red Sox all of $10,000 to sign out of Venezuela, and he's making that number look like a filing error. The glove got him here, a 60-grade defensive tool with a 55 arm, already the best defensive catcher in the system, and he's been clean behind the plate, just four passed balls in 18 starts. The bat is what's actually forcing this ranking though. He's running a 185 wRC+ between the FCL and Low-A Salem, third among every minor leaguer with at least 130 plate appearances, off a short, contact-first swing that barely strikes out.  We don’t have public exit velocity data on him, but he’s supposedly hit up to 111 max EVs, though his hard hit rate is not as consistent as we would like, keeping in mind this dude has 29 extra base hits this year in only 67 games - including 12 bombs.
ranking_explanation: He’s earned his spot in the Top 150 here with amazing hit skills and the biggest question I have at this point is if he can course correct on the angles to get more lift and what kind of consistent exit velocities are we getting from this kid.

comp: Bryce Harper mechanics, Chase DeLauter outcomes
prime_skills: Garcia is an unusual profile for a 6-3, 195-pound frame with considerable strength, exit velocities that were surprisingly modest for his size in the amateur data, 79th percentile in college ball, in part because a spring shoulder injury sapped some peak output, and he intentionally sells out for lift with an uphill path that's produced an identical 14-to-15 homer total in all three of his college seasons. The separator is that he does this without giving away contact, a 90% in-zone rate, 85 to 86% overall contact, and an 18% chase rate that ranks in the 93rd percentile, more career walks than strikeouts, and a .489 on-base percentage in his final college spring. He's one of a notable trio of 2026 additions for Atlanta alongside Jensen Hirschkorn and Carter Beck.
ranking_explanation: Scouts have called him hyper-selective for good reason, and the lift-and-still-make-contact profile isn't a bad one to dream on for more raw power once he's fully healthy from the shoulder issue that limited his peak exit velocities. He sits in the back half of this tier purely on zero professional innings, the underlying plate discipline data compares favorably to more experienced names ranked around him.

comp: Corbin Carroll is the dream
prime_skills: Nunez signed for three million dollars as the headline piece of Cincinnati's international class, and he's spent his pro debut treating that price tag like a floor, not a ceiling, a grand slam in his very first professional at-bat, an eight-game hitting streak straight out of the gate, and a current line sitting at .292/.431/.474 with more walks than strikeouts, a ridiculously low swinging strike rate and amazing supporting stats across the board. The swing is the whole story here: a toe tap into a short, violent load, hands cocking back just enough to whip the barrel through the zone in one clean snap, the kind of quick-twitch lefty stroke that looks like it shouldn't generate this much thunder out of a 165-pound frame and does anyway. There's a hitch in the hands right before the trigger, real evaluators have flagged it, but on a smaller, tightly-wound body like his, that hitch never gets the chance to turn into a long swing, it just loads and fires, a coiled spring with nowhere to leak energy. Add in true afterburner speed, a plus arm, and center-field instincts that already read like a five-year veteran's, and you've got a corner-to-center athlete whose bat might be catching up to the legs faster than anyone projected in January.  He’s running a near 83% contact rate paired with 24 steals in 50 DSL games with 5 bombs and 19 extra base hits.
ranking_explanation: Nunez is far away, but the hit tool, plate skills and speed all combine for a potential superstar outcome.  We won’t really know how real that is until we see how he transitions into full season ball and we get better statcast data, but in the meantime it’s worth moving him into top 150 lists and borderline top 100 just because of the upside.

comp: Vidal Brujan mechanics with an opposite-splits Ozzie Albies mash
prime_skills: Brito is an aggressive switch-hitting middle infielder who's going to run high batting averages on quick-twitch athleticism paired with a distinctly high-contact approach. The swing is pretty from the right side, but he's dramatically better as a lefty against right-handed pitching, star-caliber numbers on that side, while he's basically just surviving from the right side of the plate, a specific, significant platoon split worth flagging directly. He's reportedly maxed out at just a 105.2 mph exit velocity, with a solid-for-his-age 103 mph 90th-percentile reading, and he profiles much better as a high-contact doubles hitter since he doesn't get to optimal power angles, an over-50% ground-ball rate. He gets to power far more easily from the left side, seeing the ball deep and getting out in front, while as a righty he's consistently behind the pitch and making worse contact. He has an impressive 46 extra-base hits in 107 games, and while he posts plus-plus run times, he's not especially deft on the bases with average-ish SB rates.
ranking_explanation: He's got a little too much stride in his swing for my liking, and he doesn't have the balance of his own organization-mate Cristian Arguelles elsewhere on this list, a distinct mechanical gap between two switch-hitting Rockies farmhands worth remembering when comparing the two. The right-side platoon hole is the single biggest swing skill separating him from a full-time everyday profile rather than a strong-side specialist and while the ceiling appears a bit light on the tool grades, he is performing incredibly well on a back of the baseball card standpoint well under age-to-level.

comp: Royce Lewis mechanics w/ Carson Williams skillset
prime_skills: His explosive 6-2 frame produces some of the loudest raw power among middle infielders in his draft class, regularly topping 112 mph exit velocity, and the non-conference numbers were video-game stuff, a 93.8 mph average exit velocity and a 27.7% barrel rate as an amateur. The profile took a tangible hit once SEC pitching got involved though, dropping to an 89.8 mph average exit velocity and a 20.3% barrel rate, and that contact-quality split is the whole story here, an overall contact rate around 71.7 to 73.5% that's actually an improvement over a class-worst 70.4% mark a year prior, but a 43% whiff rate specifically against changeups that got exposed hard against SEC arms.  Lebron is off to a ridiculous start and he completely skipped low A (which is unfriendly to us, because we would have gotten some exit velocity data at Daytona), he’s boom or bust and right now he’s all boom.  He’s getting into some great pull angles and the 74% contact rate is certainly something we can live with his tools.
ranking_explanation: Lebron’s outcome will fully depend on his ability to achieve moderate level contact rates and keep strikeouts down to a manageable level.  He has a similar profile to a lot of other Reds middle infielders like Tyson Lewis and Matt McLain, but the swing mechanics are closer to that of Royce Lewis.  His profile is actually a little safer than Carson Williams for now and hopefully he is able to adjust and adapt the hit tool.  If he can get to a 50 hit tool and 50 plate approach, he could be a fantasy darling.

comp: Max Muncy mechanics in a Jose Ramirez-like build
prime_skills: Pena has an elite ability to get to pull-side air for his age with a very simple, quiet swing from the left side. He's a built dude for a 5-10 shortstop, considerable present strength, with the potential for a plus hit tool paired with slightly below-average pure contactability but tangibly plus quality of contact when he connects. He's gotten up to a 109.1 mph max exit velocity, though the 90th-percentile and average readings remain underwhelming so far, a wide gap between his ceiling and his typical contact. I caught many live looks this year, and while the swing and plate approach both looked good, I didn't see much actual damage or opportunities for him to run on the bases in that specific game, worth another look or two before locking in a firmer read. The hit tool and plate approach both grade well advanced for his age, and he's running a fair amount on the bases even with only moderate success, though the angles are just okay right now, nothing special, and he needs to get to more barrels specifically, a 3.9% barrel rate that's translated to just 28 extra-base hits in 101 games - maybe the worst ratio on this entire list.
ranking_explanation: Pena looks more like a second or third baseman than a true shortstop long-term, though that's not as important for fantasy purposes this far out from his debut. He was one of the best hitters in the DSL last season, and the hit tool and plate skills have translated nicely into a full-season Low-A look, telling evidence the underlying bat-to-ball ability is legitimate rather than complex-league-only production, especially notable given he's playing the entire season at just 18 years old at an advanced level for his age.  Pena currently rates out like Brito and Michael Arroyo as solid jack of all trade type middle infielders who might have more juice in the tank once they are a at a more age appropriate level for their development.

comp: Tyler O’Neil mashed with a righty Bobby Bonilla
prime_skills: Jordan's hands are the carrying tool, top-of-the-scale, lightning quick, producing titanic blasts to all fields rather than just a pull-side masher's pop, some of the best raw exit velocity data in his entire draft class when he actually connects. He's a powerfully built 6-0, 220 former three-star football recruit at Mississippi State as a wide receiver.  Jordan is an athletic freak with big time power, but he needs to work on optimization of the hit tool.  Jordan is a big bodied righty for a barely (if even)  6’0 dude with a high hands power stance that generates 118-119 max EVs and a 108.4 90th EV last year that was better than Bryce Eldridge.  If I was a coach I would teach him to keep those hands back more as he ends up getting on top of the ball a little too much in a Yandy Diaz like-way, but his lower contact rates (below 70%) limit his overall upside.  He’s very aggressive and the contact rates are fine if he were able to get to more consistent power angles.  He has fast hands and needs to adjust swing path to maximize his skillset.  He has 45 extra base hits this season in 90 games, which is an excellent pace and when healthy even with the swing and miss he’s been able to create a lot of damage.  There might be too much Colby Thomas in the profile where he dominates up until the majors, but can’t handle MLB pitching, so keep an eye on the plate skill metrics even as he produces up levels.
ranking_explanation: The power-speed foundation here is loud enough that even a moderate hit-tool improvement unlocks a legitimate fantasy asset, but the swinging-strike rate is the specific number to track, not the batting average, since that's the leading indicator of whether SEC-level pitch recognition ever catches up to the bat speed. He sits behind more finished college bats in this tier purely on that unresolved swing-and-miss question, not on the strength of the tools themselves.

comp: Kenny Lofton Lite
prime_skills: Kepley is likely to be a fast mover for the Cubs, their 2025 second-rounder known specifically for speed and defense. The wheels have really been on display this season, 60 steals in 107 minor league games and caught just five times across his entire minor league career, an elite success rate rather than pure volume. The hit tool has been legitimately phenomenal too, an 86% contact rate this year following an 85% mark last season, plenty of line drives producing a near-neutral XBH-plus mark, which is exactly what you want from a speed-first player rather than a red flag. He's a smaller guy and unlikely to develop much beyond 10-homer power, but he nets a considerable amount of liners and pairs it with a legitimately elite plate approach on top of the hit and speed tools, a complete offensive skill set even without over-the-fence pop. He walks significantly more than he strikes out and has an excellent hit tool from a contact perspective, though that contact too often translates into lightly hit flyballs.
ranking_explanation: A 70-grade present speed tool paired with a legitimately elite plate approach is a full-time leadoff-caliber outcome even in a worst-case power scenario, the hit tool alone at 60/65 present-to-future is advanced enough to carry a lineup spot on its own. He's blocked long-term in center by Pete Crow-Armstrong at the big league level, which is exactly the kind of organizational logjam that turns a player like this into a trade chip before he ever debuts in Chicago, but the Cubs do have the ability to play Kepley at a corner position which will give them a ridiculous defensive tandem in the outfield.  The power limits his ultimate upside in many fantasy leagues and Kepley will be a better real life player than fantasy asset.

comp: Smaller Oneil Cruz
prime_skills: Peete is an athletic former shortstop and third base prospect who's now playing center field for the Cardinals after they acquired him from the Mariners as part of the Brendan Donovan trade. The lefty hitter has some considerable contact concerns that haven't improved much, exposed this spring in Jupiter where I saw him live quite a few times, but the power and speed are the standout tools. We don't have full Statcast data on him this year, but he did record a 111 mph exit velocity on a homer during Spring Training. Peete gets to good angles on the ball as a high pull line-drive guy, but the contact rate hovers between 65 and 70%, thus the imbalance in his hit-tool profile. He's shown the ability to take a walk, but he chases outside the zone too much and needs to work on his plate approach. He has 11 homers and 14 steals in just 59 games so far this year, including 35 extra-base hits (a scorching damage creation pace), and while he's fast, he's a little reckless on the bases and needs to refine his baserunning instincts.
ranking_explanation: This is a true boom-or-bust profile, plausible 25-homer, 25-steal upside at a premium defensive spot (he does have a great glove) if the contact rate ever climbs into even average territory. He sits behind more finished bats in this tier purely because the swing-and-miss risk is specific enough (17% swinging strike rate), chasing out of the zone against advanced velocity, that it could plausibly cap him as a bench outfielder if it never resolves.

comp: Jakob Marsee
prime_skills: Overn was part of the return Tampa Bay got from Baltimore in the Shane Baz trade, packaged with Caden Bodine, Slater de Brun and Michael Forret elsewhere on this list plus a competitive-balance pick, telling evidence of how much value the Rays extracted from that one deal. He carries a fun power-speed combination heavy on the speed side, but a lackluster hit tool might ultimately relegate him to fourth-outfielder duty if it doesn't sharpen up. There's no public exit-velocity data on him yet, though he already gets to an above-average number of extra-base hits with 29 extra base hits in 64 games and his contact rate has improved over time (against righties). Like Marsee, he runs distinctly passive, just a 39% swing rate and he has atrocious splits against lefties that off the bat makes him a strong-side platoon hitter even in his best case outcome.
ranking_explanation: A speed-and-defense outfielder who was good enough to be a headline piece of a return for a big league starter is worth more attention than a typical honorable-mention name gets. His fScore still lags his tools given the passive approach and unresolved hit tool, but the speed with tangible defensive value is a fine floor in deeper daily leagues even in a worst-case power outcome.

comp: A mini switch-hitting Shohei Ohtani mechanically, with an Ozzie Albies-like offensive profile
prime_skills: Estrada is a small, 5-8 switch-hitting shortstop who debuted at Double-A as a 20-year-old with a solid hit tool built on above-average contact rates and a legitimately plus angles profile. The power is developing nicely, a 24.6% line-drive rate and a fantastic 128 XBH-plus mark last year, though he still needs to improve his air-pull rate to unlock more of it. He hits the ball far harder than you'd expect for a small guy, touching both a 110 and a 112 mph max exit velocity at different points this year, tangible evidence of legitimate bat speed packed into a compact frame. He's heating up at Double-A for Baltimore with an improving pull rate, though he's hitting the ball on the ground too often this year and the stolen-base totals have slowed some, he has 44 extra base hits in 107 games this year and has developed some noticeable split concerns against lefties as a switch hitter.  He’s well below average from the right side of the plate while performing excellently as a lefty against righties.  He makes enough contact to avoid strikeouts and is pretty aggressive at the plate (maybe a little too aggressive).
ranking_explanation: I love Estrada's swing, high hands, a simple toe tap in the box, and a load that gets him into far more power than his frame would suggest, mechanically calling to mind a mini switch-hitting Ohtani. I'd like him even more in a different organization, he's blocked at the position by both Jackson Holliday and Gunnar Henderson in Baltimore's system, so a trade may ultimately be what unlocks a clear path to playing time here, though he ultimately might settle in as a super utility type that plays multiple positions almost daily.

comp: A righty-hitting Gleyber Torres w/ Isaac Paredes pull power
prime_skills: Baez arrived from the Mets in last summer's Ryan Helsley trade and finished that year on a rough note, .233 with four homers in 111 at-bats at High-A Peoria, exactly the kind of quiet transition that gets a name overlooked. His age-21 season has been the opposite of quiet. He opened this year with 14 homers in just 54 games at Peoria before forcing a promotion to Double-A Springfield, and the power has only gotten louder since, a team-leading 20 homers in his first 43 Double-A games alone, seven of them coming in a nine-game stretch. His signature moment came against Arkansas, four home runs in a single day, one closing out a suspended game and three more in the nightcap for his first career three-homer outing, a game that also included back-to-back blasts with organization-mate Rainiel Rodriguez not once but twice. He's now up to 34 homers combined across both levels, now tied with fellow prospect Joshua Baez for the minor league lead, while pacing the system in RBIs and sitting second in both slugging and OPS.  We don’t have trackman at AA, but with the data we do have he’s tapped out around 108 mph max EV, but he’s getting to plus power angles and obviously has hit the ball hard consistently this season with 50 extra base hits in 97 games despite a .236 BABIP holding him down.  Baez has some weird reverse split issues against lefties that he hopefully can work out
ranking_explanation: A 55-grade power tool finally arriving in games at Double-A, and arriving loudly, is exactly the kind of second-half surge that should move a name several tiers rather than one or two spots. He closes out this batch on pure recency, this performance is happening right now, not a February projection, and a four-homer day against a Double-A opponent is as strong a current signal as anything else in this tier.  The back of the baseball card production has been excellent, but is largely based on pull power angles that he might not be able to repeat at other levels.
